lessons.title: Reversible Reactions and Dynamic Equilibrium
lessons.notes_html:
Many physical and chemical changes take place around us. Some changes can be reversed and some cannot. In this lesson we will understand reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium.

Reversible Reaction

A reaction which never goes to completion and proceeds in both the forward and the reverse directions is called a reversible reaction. It is represented by a double arrow <=>.

  • Melting of ice to form water and freezing of water to form ice is a reversible change.
  • Condensation, evaporation, freezing and melting are reversible changes.
  • Example: N2 + O2 <=> 2NO — the forward reaction forms NO from N2 + O2 and the reverse reaction forms N2 + O2 again from NO.

Irreversible Reaction

A reaction which proceeds in only one direction and goes to completion is called an irreversible reaction. It is represented by a single arrow ->. Example: burning of fuel (combustion) and rusting of iron.

Reversible ReactionIrreversible Reaction
Proceeds in both directionsProceeds in only one direction
Never goes to completionGoes to completion
Represented by double arrow <=>Represented by single arrow ->
Can establish equilibriumDoes not establish equilibrium

Chemical Equilibrium

Chemical equilibrium is the state in which, in a reversible reaction in a closed container, the rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the reverse reaction and the concentrations of the reactants and products stay constant. Example: H2 + I2 <=> 2HI.

Why Is Equilibrium Dynamic?

  • At equilibrium the two reactions do not stop.
  • The forward and reverse reactions keep going at equal rates.
  • No change is seen from outside, but internally the reaction continues.
  • Equilibrium can be reached from either side.
  • Equilibrium can be disturbed by external stress.

Equilibrium in Our Body

Equilibrium is also present in our body. Haemoglobin is a large molecule which carries oxygen to the whole body. Haemoglobin has to both pick up oxygen and release it, and this work takes place at different places in the body through changes in the chemical equilibrium of this reaction.

mcqs.q: What is a reversible reaction?
options: A reaction that goes to completion in one direction
A reaction that never goes to completion and proceeds in both the forward and reverse directions
A reaction that only takes place in a closed container
A reaction in which no products are formed
mcqs.why: A reversible reaction never goes to completion and proceeds in both the forward and the reverse directions. Because of this two-way nature it is represented by a double arrow and can establish equilibrium.

mcqs.q: By which symbol is a reversible reaction represented?
mcqs.why: A reversible reaction is represented by a double arrow, showing that it proceeds in both directions. An irreversible reaction, by contrast, is represented by a single arrow because it proceeds in only one direction.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a reversible change?
options: Melting of ice to form water
mcqs.why: Melting of ice to form water is a reversible change, because the water can freeze back into ice. Condensation, evaporation, freezing and melting are all reversible changes, while burning and rusting cannot be reversed.

mcqs.q: In the reaction N2 + O2 <=> 2NO, what does the reverse reaction form?
options: N2 and O2 again from NO
mcqs.why: In N2 + O2 <=> 2NO, the forward reaction forms NO from N2 and O2, while the reverse reaction forms N2 and O2 again from NO. This two-way conversion is exactly what makes the reaction reversible.

mcqs.q: Which statement about an irreversible reaction is correct?
options: It proceeds in only one direction and goes to completion
mcqs.why: An irreversible reaction proceeds in only one direction and goes to completion, and it is represented by a single arrow. Burning of fuel (combustion) and rusting of iron are examples of irreversible reactions.

mcqs.q: Which of the following can establish equilibrium?
mcqs.why: Only a reversible reaction can establish equilibrium, because its forward and reverse reactions can balance each other. An irreversible reaction goes to completion in one direction, so it does not establish equilibrium.

mcqs.q: What is chemical equilibrium?
options: The state in which all reactants are used up
The state in which the reaction stops completely
The state in which products are formed fastest
The state in which the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction and the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant
mcqs.why: Chemical equilibrium is the state in a reversible reaction in a closed container where the rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the reverse reaction. At this point the concentrations of the reactants and products stay constant.

mcqs.q: Which reaction is given in the notes as an example of chemical equilibrium?
mcqs.why: The notes give H2 + I2 <=> 2HI as the example of chemical equilibrium. In this reversible reaction the forward and reverse rates become equal and the concentrations stay constant.

mcqs.q: Why is equilibrium called dynamic?
options: Because the concentrations keep changing rapidly
Because at equilibrium the two reactions do not stop; the forward and reverse reactions keep going at equal rates
Because equilibrium can never be disturbed
Because the reaction vessel keeps moving
mcqs.why: Equilibrium is dynamic because the forward and reverse reactions do not stop at equilibrium; they keep going at equal rates. No change is seen from outside, but internally the reaction continues.

mcqs.q: What role does haemoglobin play in the body, as described in the notes?
options: It digests food in the stomach
It carries oxygen to the whole body, picking up and releasing it at different places through changes in chemical equilibrium
It produces heat to keep the body warm
It filters waste from the blood
mcqs.why: Haemoglobin is a large molecule which carries oxygen to the whole body. It has to both pick up oxygen and release it, and this work takes place at different places in the body through changes in the chemical equilibrium of this reaction.

lessons.title: Law of Mass Action and Expression of Equilibrium Constant
lessons.notes_html:
Active Mass

Active mass is the molar concentration of a reacting substance. Its unit is mol dm^-3 and it is written in square brackets, for example [H2].

Law of Mass Action

At any instant, the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants at that instant.

Deriving the Expression for Kc

For the general reaction: aA + bB <=> cC + dD

  • Rate of forward reaction = kf [A]^a [B]^b
  • Rate of reverse reaction = kr [C]^c [D]^d
  • At equilibrium the two rates are equal: kf [A]^a [B]^b = kr [C]^c [D]^d
  • Therefore Kc = kf / kr = [C]^c [D]^d / [A]^a [B]^b

That is, in Kc the concentrations of the products raised to the power of their coefficients are written on top and the concentrations of the reactants raised to the power of their coefficients are written below.

Examples

  • For S + O2 <=> SO2: Kc = [SO2] / [S] [O2]
  • For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3: Kc = [NH3]^2 / [N2] [H2]^3
  • For 4NH3 + 5O2 <=> 4NO + 6H2O: Kc = [NO]^4 [H2O]^6 / [NH3]^4 [O2]^5

Reaction Quotient Qc

Qc is the ratio of the molar concentrations of products and reactants raised to the power of the coefficients, but it is measured at any particular instant, not necessarily at equilibrium. Example: for H2 + I2 <=> 2HI, Kc = 48 (at 717 K). If [H2] = 0.2, [I2] = 0.2 and [HI] = 0.6 mol dm^-3, then Qc = [HI]^2 / [H2] [I2] = 0.36 / 0.04 = 9.

mcqs.q: What is active mass?
options: The total mass of a substance in grams
The molar concentration of a reacting substance
The mass of the products formed
The density of a reacting substance
mcqs.why: Active mass is the molar concentration of a reacting substance. Its unit is mol dm^-3 and it is written in square brackets, for example [H2] for hydrogen.

mcqs.q: How is the active mass of hydrogen written, and what is its unit?
mcqs.why: The active mass of a substance is written in square brackets, so hydrogen is written as [H2]. Its unit is mol dm^-3, because active mass means molar concentration.

mcqs.q: According to the law of mass action, the rate of a chemical reaction at any instant is directly proportional to what?
options: The temperature of the reaction mixture
The product of the active masses of the products
The sum of the active masses of the reactants
The product of the active masses of the reactants at that instant
mcqs.why: The law of mass action states that at any instant, the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants at that instant. It is the reactants, multiplied together, that fix the rate.

mcqs.q: For the reaction aA + bB <=> cC + dD, what is the rate of the forward reaction?
mcqs.why: The rate of the forward reaction is kf [A]^a [B]^b, using the active masses of the reactants A and B raised to their coefficients. The reverse rate instead uses the products: kr [C]^c [D]^d.

mcqs.q: At equilibrium, what relation holds between kf, kr and the concentrations?
options: kf is always greater than kr
mcqs.why: At equilibrium the two rates are equal, so kf [A]^a [B]^b = kr [C]^c [D]^d. Rearranging this equality gives Kc = kf / kr = [C]^c [D]^d / [A]^a [B]^b.

mcqs.q: What is the value of Kc in terms of the rate constants?
mcqs.why: From the equilibrium condition, Kc = kf / kr, the ratio of the forward rate constant to the reverse rate constant. This same Kc also equals the product concentrations over the reactant concentrations, each raised to its coefficient.

mcqs.q: In the expression for Kc, how are the concentrations arranged?
options: Reactants on top and products below, without powers
Products raised to their coefficients on top and reactants raised to their coefficients below
Only the gaseous substances are included
mcqs.why: In Kc the concentrations of the products raised to the power of their coefficients are written on top, and the concentrations of the reactants raised to the power of their coefficients are written below. This pattern is followed in every Kc expression.

mcqs.q: For S + O2 <=> SO2, what is Kc?
mcqs.why: For S + O2 <=> SO2, the product SO2 goes on top and the reactants S and O2 go below, giving Kc = [SO2] / [S] [O2]. All coefficients here are 1, so no powers appear in the expression.

mcqs.q: For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, what is Kc?
mcqs.why: For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, Kc = [NH3]^2 / [N2] [H2]^3. The power 2 on NH3 and the power 3 on H2 come directly from their coefficients in the balanced equation.

mcqs.q: For H2 + I2 <=> 2HI with [H2] = 0.2, [I2] = 0.2 and [HI] = 0.6 mol dm^-3, what is Qc, and how does Qc differ from Kc?
options: Qc = 9, and it is measured at any particular instant, not necessarily at equilibrium
Qc = 48, and it is measured only at equilibrium
Qc = 0.11, and it is measured only at 717 K
Qc = 3, and it never changes with time
mcqs.why: Qc = [HI]^2 / [H2] [I2] = 0.36 / 0.04 = 9. Unlike Kc, which applies at equilibrium (here Kc = 48 at 717 K), Qc is the same ratio measured at any particular instant, not necessarily at equilibrium.

lessons.title: Equilibrium Constant and Its Units
lessons.notes_html:
Characteristics of Kc

  • Kc works only at equilibrium.
  • It expresses the equilibrium concentrations of reactants and products in mol dm^-3.
  • It is independent of the initial concentrations.
  • It changes with temperature, and temperature is the single factor affecting its value.
  • Kc tells both the direction and the extent of the reaction.

When Does Kc Have a Unit?

Whether Kc has a unit depends on whether the numbers of moles on the two sides are equal or not.

ConditionExampleUnit of Kc
Moles on both sides are equalN2 + O2 <=> 2NONo unit
Moles on both sides are not equalN2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3mol^-2 dm^6
Two moles of product from one moleN2O4 <=> 2NO2mol dm^-3

Worked Example 1

For N2O4 <=> 2NO2, Kc = [NO2]^2 / [N2O4]. Unit: the top has mol dm^-3 squared and the bottom has mol dm^-3, so the unit of Kc is mol dm^-3.

Worked Example 2

For PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2, at 500 K [PCl5] = 0.8 x 10^-3, [PCl3] = 1.2 x 10^-3 and [Cl2] = 1.2 x 10^-3 mol dm^-3. Kc = [PCl3] [Cl2] / [PCl5] = (1.2 x 10^-3 x 1.2 x 10^-3) / (0.8 x 10^-3) = 1.8 x 10^-3 mol dm^-3.

mcqs.q: Kc works only under which condition?
options: At any instant of the reaction
mcqs.why: Kc works only at equilibrium, because it is defined from the equilibrium concentrations of reactants and products. The similar ratio measured at any other instant is the reaction quotient Qc, not Kc.

mcqs.q: Which statement about Kc is correct?
options: It depends on the initial concentrations
It is independent of the initial concentrations
It changes when more reactant is added at the start
It is measured in grams per litre
mcqs.why: Kc is independent of the initial concentrations of the reactants and products. It expresses the equilibrium concentrations in mol dm^-3, and its value is fixed for a given temperature.

mcqs.q: Which single factor affects the value of Kc?
mcqs.why: Kc changes with temperature, and temperature is the single factor affecting its value. Changing the initial concentrations does not change Kc; the equilibrium concentrations adjust instead.

mcqs.q: What two things does Kc tell us about a reaction?
options: The direction and the extent of the reaction
The mass and volume of the products
mcqs.why: Kc tells both the direction and the extent of the reaction. Its size shows whether the equilibrium mixture favours reactants or products and by how much.

mcqs.q: For N2 + O2 <=> 2NO, what is the unit of Kc?
mcqs.why: When the numbers of moles on both sides are equal, as in N2 + O2 <=> 2NO (2 moles on each side), Kc has no unit. The concentration units on the top and bottom cancel each other completely.

mcqs.q: For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, what is the unit of Kc?
mcqs.why: In N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3 the moles on the two sides are not equal (4 moles of reactants, 2 moles of product), so Kc has a unit. Working through the concentration powers gives the unit mol^-2 dm^6.

mcqs.q: For N2O4 <=> 2NO2, what is the unit of Kc?
mcqs.why: For N2O4 <=> 2NO2, Kc = [NO2]^2 / [N2O4], so the top has (mol dm^-3)^2 and the bottom has mol dm^-3. Dividing leaves one power, giving the unit mol dm^-3, because two moles of product form from one mole of reactant.

mcqs.q: In worked example 1, why does Kc for N2O4 <=> 2NO2 have the unit mol dm^-3?
options: Because the top has mol dm^-3 squared and the bottom has mol dm^-3, leaving mol dm^-3
Because Kc always has this unit
mcqs.why: In Kc = [NO2]^2 / [N2O4], the numerator carries (mol dm^-3)^2 while the denominator carries mol dm^-3. Cancelling one power leaves mol dm^-3 as the unit of Kc for this reaction.

mcqs.q: For PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2, what is the expression for Kc?
mcqs.why: For PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2, the products PCl3 and Cl2 are multiplied on top and the reactant PCl5 goes below, so Kc = [PCl3] [Cl2] / [PCl5]. All coefficients are 1, so no powers appear.

mcqs.q: At 500 K, [PCl5] = 0.8 x 10^-3, [PCl3] = 1.2 x 10^-3 and [Cl2] = 1.2 x 10^-3 mol dm^-3. What is Kc for PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2?
mcqs.why: Kc = [PCl3] [Cl2] / [PCl5] = (1.2 x 10^-3 x 1.2 x 10^-3) / (0.8 x 10^-3) = 1.8 x 10^-3 mol dm^-3. The numerator gives 1.44 x 10^-6, and dividing by 0.8 x 10^-3 gives 1.8 x 10^-3.

lessons.title: Importance of Equilibrium Constant
lessons.notes_html:
What Does the Magnitude of Kc Tell Us?

Magnitude of KcMeaning
Small KcThe reaction mixture mostly contains reactants
Moderate KcThe mixture contains almost equal amounts of reactants and products
Large KcThe reaction mixture mostly contains product
  • If Kc is greater than 1, the reaction is in the forward direction.
  • If Kc is less than 1, the reaction is in the reverse direction.
  • Kc tells both the direction and the extent of the reaction.

Example: Two Systems

  • For 2CO2 <=> 2CO + O2, Kc = 3.1 x 10^-18 mol dm^-3 (very small) — at equilibrium there will be mostly reactant CO2 and very little product.
  • For 2O3 <=> 3O2, Kc = 5.9 x 10^55 mol dm^-3 (very large) — at equilibrium there will be mostly product O2 and very little reactant.

Predicting Direction by Comparing Qc and Kc

ConditionResult
Qc < KcThe net reaction proceeds forward, more product is formed
Qc > KcThe net reaction proceeds in reverse, more reactants are formed
Qc = KcThe system is in equilibrium, no net change occurs

Worked Example

For 2HI <=> H2 + I2, Kc = 1 x 10^-4. If [HI] = 2 x 10^-5, [H2] = 1 x 10^-5 and [I2] = 1 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3, then Qc = [H2] [I2] / [HI]^2 = 1 x 10^-10 / 4 x 10^-10 = 0.25. Qc, that is 0.25, is greater than Kc, so the net reaction will proceed in the reverse direction and more HI will be formed.

mcqs.q: If Kc is small, what does the reaction mixture mostly contain?
options: Equal amounts of reactants and products
mcqs.why: A small Kc means the reaction mixture mostly contains reactants, because very little product is present at equilibrium. The smaller the Kc, the more the equilibrium favours the reactant side.

mcqs.q: If Kc is large, what does the reaction mixture mostly contain?
mcqs.why: A large Kc means the reaction mixture mostly contains product at equilibrium. The reaction has proceeded far in the forward direction before the forward and reverse rates became equal.

mcqs.q: If Kc is moderate, what does the mixture contain?
options: Almost equal amounts of reactants and products
mcqs.why: A moderate Kc means the mixture contains almost equal amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium. Neither side is strongly favoured when Kc is neither very small nor very large.

mcqs.q: If Kc is greater than 1, in which direction is the reaction?
mcqs.why: If Kc is greater than 1, the reaction is in the forward direction, so products dominate at equilibrium. If Kc is less than 1, the reaction is in the reverse direction and reactants dominate.

mcqs.q: For 2CO2 <=> 2CO + O2, Kc = 3.1 x 10^-18 mol dm^-3. What will the equilibrium mixture contain?
options: Mostly reactant CO2 and very little product
Equal amounts of CO2 and CO
mcqs.why: Kc = 3.1 x 10^-18 is very small, so at equilibrium there will be mostly reactant CO2 and very little product. A tiny Kc shows the reaction hardly proceeds in the forward direction.

mcqs.q: For 2O3 <=> 3O2, Kc = 5.9 x 10^55 mol dm^-3. What will the equilibrium mixture contain?
options: Mostly product O2 and very little reactant
Equal amounts of O3 and O2
mcqs.why: Kc = 5.9 x 10^55 is very large, so at equilibrium there will be mostly product O2 and very little reactant. Such a huge Kc means the forward reaction goes almost to completion.

mcqs.q: If Qc < Kc, what happens to the net reaction?
options: It proceeds in reverse and more reactants are formed
It is at equilibrium with no net change
It proceeds forward and more product is formed
mcqs.why: If Qc < Kc, the net reaction proceeds forward and more product is formed until equilibrium is reached. The product concentration is still below its equilibrium value, so the forward reaction dominates.

mcqs.q: If Qc > Kc, what happens to the net reaction?
options: It proceeds forward and more product is formed
It proceeds in reverse and more reactants are formed
More product and more reactants form equally
mcqs.why: If Qc > Kc, the net reaction proceeds in the reverse direction and more reactants are formed. This continues until Qc falls to equal Kc and the system reaches equilibrium.

mcqs.q: If Qc = Kc, what is the state of the system?
options: The system is in equilibrium and no net change occurs
The reaction runs forward very fast
The reaction runs in reverse very fast
mcqs.why: If Qc = Kc, the system is in equilibrium and no net change occurs. The forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so the concentrations stay constant.

mcqs.q: For 2HI <=> H2 + I2, Kc = 1 x 10^-4 and the calculated Qc = 0.25. In which direction will the net reaction proceed?
options: Forward, forming more H2 and I2
mcqs.why: Qc = [H2] [I2] / [HI]^2 = 1 x 10^-10 / 4 x 10^-10 = 0.25, which is greater than Kc = 1 x 10^-4. Since Qc > Kc, the net reaction proceeds in the reverse direction and more HI will be formed.

lessons.title: Concepts of Acids and Bases
lessons.notes_html:
Properties of Acids and Bases

AcidsBases
Sour in tasteBitter in taste
Give H+ in aqueous solutionGive OH- in aqueous solution
Turn blue litmus paper redTurn red litmus paper blue
Have a corrosive effectFeel soapy

Note: Both acids and bases can have a corrosive effect on the skin.

Arrhenius Concept

According to Arrhenius, an acid is one that gives H+ in aqueous solution, for example HCl -> H+ + Cl-, and a base is one that gives OH- in aqueous solution, for example NaOH -> Na+ + OH-. This theory is only applicable to aqueous solutions, because without water these ions are not formed. For example, CO2 is not an Arrhenius acid.

Bronsted-Lowry Concept

According to this theory, an acid is a proton (H+) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. Example: In HCl + NH3 -> NH4+ + Cl-, HCl donates a proton so it is the acid, and NH3 accepts a proton so it is the base. According to this theory NH3 can be a base, even though it does not contain OH-.

Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs

  • When an acid donates a proton, what remains is its conjugate base: the conjugate base of HCl is Cl-.
  • When a base accepts a proton, what forms is its conjugate acid: the conjugate acid of NH3 is NH4+.
  • The conjugate base of H2SO4 is HSO4- and the conjugate acid of H2O is H3O+.
  • Water is amphoteric: it has both a conjugate acid H3O+ and a conjugate base OH-.

Lewis Concept

According to Lewis, a base is one that can donate a pair of electrons to form a coordinate covalent bond, and an acid is one that accepts a pair of electrons. Example: CN- is a Lewis base. NH3 is a base according to both the Bronsted-Lowry and Lewis theories.

Amphoteric Substances

Substances that react with both acids and bases are called amphoteric substances. Water is an important example of this.

mcqs.q: Which set of properties belongs to acids?
options: Bitter in taste, give OH- in aqueous solution
Sour in taste, give H+ in aqueous solution, turn blue litmus paper red
Feel soapy and turn red litmus paper blue
Have no effect on litmus paper
mcqs.why: Acids are sour in taste, give H+ in aqueous solution and turn blue litmus paper red. Bases, in contrast, are bitter in taste, give OH- in aqueous solution, turn red litmus paper blue and feel soapy.

mcqs.q: What do bases do to litmus paper, and how do they feel?
options: They turn blue litmus paper red and feel rough
They do not change litmus paper and feel sticky
They bleach litmus paper and feel dry
They turn red litmus paper blue and feel soapy
mcqs.why: Bases turn red litmus paper blue and feel soapy to the touch. They are bitter in taste and give OH- in aqueous solution, the opposite pattern to acids.

mcqs.q: According to Arrhenius, what is an acid? Give the example from the notes.
options: A proton donor, for example NH3
A substance that accepts an electron pair, for example CN-
One that gives H+ in aqueous solution, for example HCl -> H+ + Cl-
One that gives OH- in aqueous solution, for example NaOH
mcqs.why: According to Arrhenius, an acid is one that gives H+ in aqueous solution, for example HCl -> H+ + Cl-. An Arrhenius base gives OH- in aqueous solution, for example NaOH -> Na+ + OH-.

mcqs.q: What is the limitation of the Arrhenius concept?
options: It is only applicable to aqueous solutions, because without water these ions are not formed; for example CO2 is not an Arrhenius acid
It cannot explain the behaviour of HCl
It works only at high temperature
mcqs.why: The Arrhenius theory is only applicable to aqueous solutions, because without water the H+ and OH- ions are not formed. For this reason CO2 is not an Arrhenius acid, even though it behaves as an acid in water.

mcqs.q: According to the Bronsted-Lowry concept, what is an acid and what is a base?
options: An acid is a proton (H+) donor and a base is a proton acceptor
An acid accepts a proton and a base donates a proton
An acid gives OH- and a base gives H+
mcqs.why: According to Bronsted-Lowry, an acid is a proton (H+) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. This definition does not require water or OH-, so it covers more substances than the Arrhenius concept.

mcqs.q: In HCl + NH3 -> NH4+ + Cl-, which substance is the Bronsted-Lowry base, and why?
options: HCl, because it donates a proton
Cl-, because it is formed in the reaction
NH3, because it accepts a proton
NH4+, because it carries a positive charge
mcqs.why: NH3 is the base because it accepts a proton, forming NH4+. HCl donates the proton, so HCl is the acid in this reaction according to the Bronsted-Lowry concept.

mcqs.q: What is the conjugate base of HCl?
mcqs.why: When an acid donates a proton, what remains is its conjugate base, so the conjugate base of HCl is Cl-. HCl loses its proton and the Cl- that remains is its conjugate partner.

mcqs.q: Which pair of conjugate answers is correct?
options: Conjugate acid of NH3 is NH4+ and conjugate base of H2SO4 is HSO4-
Conjugate acid of NH3 is NH2- and conjugate base of H2SO4 is SO4^2- only
Conjugate acid of H2O is OH- and conjugate base of HCl is H2Cl+
Conjugate acid of NH3 is Cl- and conjugate base of H2SO4 is H3SO4+
mcqs.why: When a base accepts a proton it forms its conjugate acid, so the conjugate acid of NH3 is NH4+. When an acid donates a proton it leaves its conjugate base, so the conjugate base of H2SO4 is HSO4-.

mcqs.q: According to Lewis, what is a base, and which example is given?
options: A base accepts a pair of electrons; CN- is an example
A base donates a pair of electrons to form a coordinate covalent bond; CN- is a Lewis base
A base gives H+ in water; HCl is an example
A base is a proton acceptor; NH4+ is an example
mcqs.why: According to Lewis, a base is one that can donate a pair of electrons to form a coordinate covalent bond, and an acid accepts a pair of electrons. CN- is given as a Lewis base, and NH3 is a base under both the Bronsted-Lowry and Lewis theories.

mcqs.q: What are amphoteric substances, and what is the important example given?
options: Substances that are neither acids nor bases; NaCl is the example
Substances that only react with acids; HCl is the example
Substances that react with both acids and bases; water is an important example
Substances that change colour in acids; litmus is the example
mcqs.why: Substances that react with both acids and bases are called amphoteric substances, and water is an important example. Water has both a conjugate acid, H3O+, and a conjugate base, OH-, which shows its dual behaviour.

lessons.title: Concept of pH and pOH
lessons.notes_html:
Ionization of Water

Pure water ionizes only very slightly, so it is considered a weak electrolyte:

  • H2O <=> H+ + OH-, or 2H2O <=> H3O+ + OH-
  • Ionization constant: Kw = [H+] [OH-] = 1 x 10^-14 (at 25 C)
  • In pure water [H+] = [OH-] = 1 x 10^-7 mol dm^-3, so its pH is 7 and it is neutral.

Definitions of pH and pOH

  • pH is the measure of the hydrogen ion concentration: pH = -log [H+]
  • pOH = -log [OH-]
  • pH + pOH = 14
Condition[H+] and [OH-]pH
Acidic solution[H+] > [OH-]Less than 7
Neutral solution[H+] = [OH-]7
Basic solution[OH-] > [H+]More than 7

pH of Everyday Things

ThingpH
Lemon juice2.3
Soda water3.8
Black coffee5.0
Milk6.3 to 6.6
Washing soda12.0

Calculation Examples

  • If a solution has [H+] = 1 x 10^-8 mol dm^-3, then pH = -log 1 x 10^-8 = 8, so the solution is basic.
  • For 5M NaOH, [OH-] = 5, pOH = -log 5 = -0.70, and pH = 14 - (-0.70) = 14.70.
  • If a solution has pH 1.05, then pOH = 14 - 1.05 = 12.95 and [H+] = 10^-1.05 = 8.9 x 10^-2 mol dm^-3.

Indicators and Titration

  • An indicator is a weak organic acid or base which changes its colour over a small range of pH.
  • Titration is a technique in which a solution of known concentration is used to determine the concentration of an unknown solution.

Buffers

A buffer is an aqueous solution which resists a change in its pH on the addition of a small amount of acid or base. The composition of a buffer is a weak acid and its salt (its conjugate base), for example CH3COOH and CH3COONa, or a weak base and its salt, for example NH3 and NH4Cl. The serum of blood stays at about pH 7.4, which is due to buffers. Preservatives are also used to preserve food.

mcqs.q: Why is pure water considered a weak electrolyte?
options: Because it ionizes completely into ions
Because it reacts strongly with acids
Because it contains no ions at all
Because it ionizes only very slightly: H2O <=> H+ + OH-
mcqs.why: Pure water ionizes only very slightly, so it is considered a weak electrolyte. Its ionization is written as H2O <=> H+ + OH-, or 2H2O <=> H3O+ + OH-.

mcqs.q: What is the ionization constant of water, Kw, at 25 C?
mcqs.why: The ionization constant of water is Kw = [H+] [OH-] = 1 x 10^-14 at 25 C. This fixed product connects the hydrogen ion and hydroxide ion concentrations in any aqueous solution at that temperature.

mcqs.q: In pure water, what are [H+] and the pH?
options: [H+] = 1 x 10^-7 mol dm^-3 and pH = 7, so it is neutral
[H+] = 1 x 10^-2 and pH = 2, so it is acidic
mcqs.why: In pure water [H+] = [OH-] = 1 x 10^-7 mol dm^-3, so its pH is 7 and it is neutral. Equal hydrogen and hydroxide ion concentrations are the condition for neutrality.

mcqs.q: How are pH and pOH defined?
mcqs.why: pH is the measure of the hydrogen ion concentration, defined as pH = -log [H+]. Similarly pOH = -log [OH-], and together they always satisfy pH + pOH = 14.

mcqs.q: What is the relation between pH and pOH?
mcqs.why: pH + pOH = 14 for an aqueous solution. So if the pH of a solution is 1.05, its pOH is 14 - 1.05 = 12.95, as shown in the calculation examples.

mcqs.q: Which condition describes an acidic solution?
mcqs.why: In an acidic solution [H+] is greater than [OH-] and the pH is less than 7. A neutral solution has [H+] = [OH-] and pH 7, while a basic solution has [OH-] > [H+] and pH more than 7.

mcqs.q: Which pH values from the notes are correct?
options: Lemon juice 2.3, black coffee 5.0, milk 6.3 to 6.6 and washing soda 12.0
mcqs.why: The notes list lemon juice at pH 2.3, soda water at 3.8, black coffee at 5.0, milk at 6.3 to 6.6 and washing soda at 12.0. Lemon juice is therefore acidic and washing soda is strongly basic.

mcqs.q: A solution has [H+] = 1 x 10^-8 mol dm^-3. What is its pH and nature?
options: pH = 8, so the solution is basic
pH = 8, so the solution is acidic
pH = -8, so the solution is basic
pH = 6, so the solution is acidic
mcqs.why: pH = -log (1 x 10^-8) = 8. Since a pH of 8 is more than 7, the solution is basic, even though the hydrogen ion concentration itself is very small.

mcqs.q: For 5M NaOH, what are the pOH and pH?
mcqs.why: For 5M NaOH, [OH-] = 5, so pOH = -log 5 = -0.70. Then pH = 14 - (-0.70) = 14.70, showing that a very concentrated base can have a pH above 14.

mcqs.q: What is a buffer, and what is it made of?
options: A solution that changes pH rapidly; made of a strong acid and its salt
A coloured solution used in titration; made of an indicator
An aqueous solution which resists a change in its pH on addition of a small amount of acid or base; made of a weak acid and its salt, for example CH3COOH and CH3COONa
A solution with pH exactly 7; made of pure water
mcqs.why: A buffer is an aqueous solution which resists a change in its pH on the addition of a small amount of acid or base. It consists of a weak acid and its salt (its conjugate base), such as CH3COOH and CH3COONa, or a weak base and its salt, such as NH3 and NH4Cl; blood serum stays at about pH 7.4 due to buffers.

lessons.title: Salts
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Salt?

A salt is an ionic compound in which the cation comes from the base and the anion comes from the acid. It is obtained along with water in the neutralization of an acid and a base. Examples: NaCl, K2SO4, KNO3, BaCl2 and KCl are salts, whereas HCl and HNO3 are acids and NaOH and KOH are bases.

Neutralization

The reaction of an acid and a base to form salt and water is called neutralization. Balancing it means that the H+ obtained from the acid and the OH- obtained from the base are in equal numbers:

  • NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O (one H+ and one OH-)
  • 2NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O (2NaOH to make two H+ and two OH- equal)
  • Ca(OH)2 + 2HNO3 -> Ca(NO3)2 + 2H2O

Types of Salts

TypepHExamples
Acidic saltsLess than 7NH4Cl, NaHSO4
Basic saltsMore than 7CH3COONa, Na2CO3
Neutral salts7NaCl, KCl

Preparation of Salts

  • Action of acids on metals
  • Action of acids on metal oxides, metal hydroxides, metal carbonates and metal bicarbonates
  • Action of a base with an acid (neutralization)
  • Action of a metal with a base

Uses of Salts in Daily Life

  • As fertilizers in agriculture: ammonium chloride and NPK fertilizers
  • As disinfectants: copper sulphate and potassium permanganate
  • Plaster of Paris: to make plaster casts for broken bones
  • Iron sulphate: in medicine for anaemia
  • Sodium hydrogen carbonate: in medicine for stomach acidity
  • Barium sulphate: in X-rays of the stomach
  • Common salt: in food for taste and preservation

mcqs.q: What is a salt?
options: A covalent compound formed from two acids
An ionic compound in which the cation comes from the base and the anion comes from the acid
A compound obtained by heating a metal
mcqs.why: A salt is an ionic compound in which the cation comes from the base and the anion comes from the acid. It is obtained along with water in the neutralization of an acid and a base, for example NaCl.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a salt?
mcqs.why: K2SO4 is a salt, as are NaCl, KNO3, BaCl2 and KCl. HCl and HNO3 are acids, while NaOH and KOH are bases, so they are not salts.

mcqs.q: What is neutralization?
options: The reaction of a metal with an acid to give hydrogen
The reaction of an acid and a base to form salt and water
The heating of a salt to break it down
The dissolving of a salt in water
mcqs.why: Neutralization is the reaction of an acid and a base to form salt and water. Balancing it means the H+ obtained from the acid and the OH- obtained from the base are in equal numbers.

mcqs.q: What is formed in NaOH + HCl -> ?
mcqs.why: NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O, a neutralization in which the salt NaCl and water are formed. This pair supplies one H+ and one OH-, which combine to make the water molecule.

mcqs.q: Why are 2 moles of NaOH needed with H2SO4 in 2NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O?
options: To make the two H+ from the acid and the two OH- from the base equal in number
To give the salt a colour
mcqs.why: H2SO4 supplies two H+, so two NaOH are needed to supply two OH- and make the numbers equal. Only then is the neutralization balanced, giving Na2SO4 + 2H2O.

mcqs.q: What are the products of Ca(OH)2 + 2HNO3 -> ?
mcqs.why: Ca(OH)2 + 2HNO3 -> Ca(NO3)2 + 2H2O. The calcium from the base and the nitrate from the acid form the salt calcium nitrate, and the H+ and OH- combine to form two water molecules.

mcqs.q: Which salts are acidic salts, and what is their pH?
options: CH3COONa and Na2CO3, pH more than 7
NH4Cl and NaHSO4, pH less than 7
Na2SO4 and KNO3, pH more than 7
mcqs.why: Acidic salts have a pH less than 7, and the examples given are NH4Cl and NaHSO4. Basic salts such as CH3COONa and Na2CO3 have pH more than 7, while neutral salts such as NaCl and KCl have pH 7.

mcqs.q: Which statement about salt types is correct?
options: Basic salts have pH less than 7
Acidic salts have pH more than 7
Neutral salts such as NaCl and KCl have pH 7
mcqs.why: Neutral salts such as NaCl and KCl have pH 7. Acidic salts have pH less than 7 and basic salts have pH more than 7, so the type of salt decides whether its solution is acidic, basic or neutral.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a method of preparing salts given in the notes?
options: Burning of metals in air only
mcqs.why: Salts can be prepared by the action of acids on metals. Other methods listed are the action of acids on metal oxides, metal hydroxides, metal carbonates and metal bicarbonates, neutralization of a base with an acid, and the action of a metal with a base.

mcqs.q: Which use of a salt is correctly matched?
options: Copper sulphate is used for anaemia
Iron sulphate is used as plaster for bones
Barium sulphate is used in X-rays of the stomach
Common salt is used as a disinfectant only
mcqs.why: Barium sulphate is used in X-rays of the stomach. Iron sulphate is used in medicine for anaemia, Plaster of Paris is used to make plaster casts for broken bones, and copper sulphate and potassium permanganate are used as disinfectants.

lessons.title: Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
What is Organic Chemistry?

The branch of chemistry which deals with hydrocarbons and their derivatives is called organic chemistry. Carbon is an essential element in organic compounds.

Vital Force Theory

According to the old idea, organic compounds can only be prepared in living tissues by a vital force and cannot be prepared in the laboratory. This is called the Vital Force Theory.

Catenation

Catenation is the ability of carbon atoms to join with one another through covalent bonds to form long chains or rings. Examples: in ethane two carbon atoms are joined to each other; in pentane there is a chain of five carbon atoms; in cyclohexane carbon atoms are joined in a ring. Carbon has a much greater power of catenation than silicon, because the C-C bond, at 355 kJ mol^-1, is much stronger than the Si-Si bond at 200 kJ mol^-1. Silicon is found in nature as silica and silicates, because the Si-O bond, at 452 kJ mol^-1, is stronger than the C-O bond at 351 kJ mol^-1.

Diversity and Magnitude of Organic Compounds

Organic compounds are very many and of very many kinds: more than 10 million organic compounds exist, far more than the compounds of all the other elements. The reasons are: catenation, isomerism, the strong covalent bonds of carbon, and the ability to form multiple bonds.

Important Characteristics of Organic Compounds

  • Carbon is an essential element in them and they are derivatives of hydrocarbons.
  • They dissolve in organic solvents.
  • Their covalent bonds are weaker than ionic bonds, so they have low melting and boiling points.
  • Their rate of reaction is slow, because their covalent bonds take time to break and need more energy; in contrast, ionic compounds react fast.
  • On combustion, all organic compounds give carbon dioxide.
  • Many organic compounds are used in perfumes, dyes and drugs.

Homologous Series

A homologous series is a group of compounds whose members have the same functional group, the same general formula, and differ from one another by CH2. Common series are: alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, alcohols and carboxylic acids.

mcqs.q: What is organic chemistry?
options: The branch of chemistry that deals with hydrocarbons and their derivatives
The branch of chemistry that deals only with metals and their ores
The branch of chemistry that deals with salts dissolved in water
The branch of chemistry that deals with gases in the atmosphere
mcqs.why: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry which deals with hydrocarbons and their derivatives. Carbon is an essential element in all organic compounds, which is why this branch is centred on carbon compounds.

mcqs.q: Which element is essential in organic compounds?
mcqs.why: Carbon is an essential element in organic compounds, and organic compounds are derivatives of hydrocarbons. No organic compound exists without carbon, whereas silicon, oxygen or nitrogen are not essential in every one of them.

mcqs.q: According to the Vital Force Theory, organic compounds could be prepared only:
options: In a laboratory using strong acids
By heating minerals at high temperature
In living tissues by a vital force
mcqs.why: The Vital Force Theory was the old idea that organic compounds can only be prepared in living tissues by a vital force. According to this theory they could not be prepared in the laboratory, which is why the other options are wrong.

mcqs.q: Catenation is the ability of carbon atoms to:
options: Break down into ions in water
Join with one another through covalent bonds to form long chains or rings
mcqs.why: Catenation is the ability of carbon atoms to join with one another through covalent bonds to form long chains or rings. For example, two carbon atoms are joined in ethane, five form a chain in pentane, and the carbons form a ring in cyclohexane.

mcqs.q: The C-C bond energy is 355 kJ mol-1, while the Si-Si bond energy is only:
mcqs.why: The C-C bond, at 355 kJ mol-1, is much stronger than the Si-Si bond at 200 kJ mol-1. Because of this, carbon has a much greater power of catenation than silicon, since its atoms stay firmly joined in chains.

mcqs.q: Silicon is found in nature as silica and silicates because:
options: The Si-Si bond is stronger than the C-C bond
The Si-O bond (452 kJ mol-1) is stronger than the C-O bond (351 kJ mol-1)
Silicon cannot form any covalent bonds
Silicon atoms form longer chains than carbon atoms
mcqs.why: The Si-O bond, at 452 kJ mol-1, is stronger than the C-O bond at 351 kJ mol-1. Because silicon bonds so strongly to oxygen, silicon is found in nature as silica and silicates rather than in long self-chains.

mcqs.q: How many organic compounds are known to exist?
mcqs.why: More than 10 million organic compounds exist, far more than the compounds of all the other elements combined. This huge number is one of the striking features of organic chemistry and comes from the special behaviour of carbon.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a reason for the great diversity of organic compounds?
mcqs.why: Catenation is one of the reasons for the diversity and magnitude of organic compounds, along with isomerism, the strong covalent bonds of carbon and its ability to form multiple bonds. Organic compounds actually have low melting points and slow reactions, so those options are wrong.

mcqs.q: On combustion, all organic compounds give:
mcqs.why: On combustion, all organic compounds give carbon dioxide. This is listed among the important characteristics of organic compounds, together with their solubility in organic solvents and their low melting and boiling points.

mcqs.q: Members of a homologous series have the same functional group and general formula, and differ from one another by:
mcqs.why: A homologous series is a group of compounds whose members have the same functional group and the same general formula, and differ from one another by CH2. Alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, alcohols and carboxylic acids are common examples of such series.

lessons.title: Sources of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Main Sources

There are two main sources of organic compounds: living things and minerals.

  • From living things: animals give proteins and fats, and plants give carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins and oils.
  • From minerals: coal, petroleum and natural gas are obtained.

Coal

Coal is formed from trees buried in the earth. The percentage of carbon in it increases with its grade:

TypeCarbon
Wood40 percent
Peat60 percent
Lignite70 percent
Anthracite90 percent

Petroleum

Petroleum is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons formed underground from dead plants and animals. It is separated by fractional distillation into separate useful fractions, for example petrol, kerosene and diesel, all of which are organic compounds.

Natural Gas

Natural gas is mostly methane. In Pakistan it is called Sui gas.

mcqs.q: The two main sources of organic compounds are:
mcqs.why: There are two main sources of organic compounds: living things and minerals. Animals and plants supply many organic compounds, while coal, petroleum and natural gas are obtained from minerals.

mcqs.q: Animals give us which organic compounds?
mcqs.why: From living things, animals give proteins and fats. Plants, on the other hand, give carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins and oils, so starch and cellulose are plant products, not the animal contribution named in the notes.

mcqs.q: Plants give which set of organic compounds?
mcqs.why: Plants give carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins and oils. Coal, petroleum and natural gas come from the mineral source instead, so they do not belong to the list of things obtained directly from plants.

mcqs.q: Coal is formed from:
mcqs.why: Coal is formed from trees buried in the earth. The percentage of carbon in coal increases with its grade, rising from wood through peat and lignite up to anthracite.

mcqs.q: What is the percentage of carbon in peat?
mcqs.why: Peat contains 60 percent carbon. In comparison, wood has 40 percent, lignite has 70 percent and anthracite has 90 percent carbon, showing how the carbon content rises with the grade of the fuel.

mcqs.q: Lignite contains what percentage of carbon?
mcqs.why: Lignite contains 70 percent carbon, which places it between peat at 60 percent and anthracite at 90 percent. Wood, the starting material, contains only 40 percent carbon.

mcqs.q: Which form of coal contains the highest percentage of carbon, 90 percent?
mcqs.why: Anthracite contains 90 percent carbon, the highest of the grades listed. The carbon percentage increases with grade: wood 40 percent, peat 60 percent, lignite 70 percent and anthracite 90 percent.

mcqs.q: Petroleum is separated into useful fractions such as petrol, kerosene and diesel by:
mcqs.why: Petroleum is separated by fractional distillation into separate useful fractions, for example petrol, kerosene and diesel. All of these fractions are organic compounds obtained from the same complex mixture of hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: Petroleum is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons formed underground from:
mcqs.why: Petroleum is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons formed underground from dead plants and animals. It is obtained from the mineral source of organic compounds, along with coal and natural gas.

mcqs.q: Natural gas is mostly methane, and in Pakistan it is called:
mcqs.why: Natural gas is mostly methane, and in Pakistan it is called Sui gas. It is one of the mineral sources of organic compounds, together with coal and petroleum.

lessons.title: Uses of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
General Uses

Organic compounds are used everywhere in our daily life:

  • As food
  • As clothing
  • As houses (shelter)
  • As fuel
  • As medicines
  • As raw materials

Industrial Uses

  • In making perfumes
  • In making dyes
  • In making soaps
  • In making plastics — polyethene is a plastic
  • In making drugs

Role of the Pharmaceutical Chemist

The pharmaceutical chemist plays an important role in laboratory analysis, quality assurance and the production of new effective drugs.

Compounds from Natural Sources

  • Acetic acid is obtained from vinegar.
  • Petrol, diesel and kerosene are used as fuel, all of which are organic compounds.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a daily-life use of organic compounds?
options: As electric insulators in power stations only
mcqs.why: Organic compounds are used everywhere in daily life, including as fuel. They are also used as food, clothing, shelter, medicines and raw materials, which shows how wide their everyday role is.

mcqs.q: Polyethene is an example of:
mcqs.why: Polyethene is a plastic, and making plastics is one of the industrial uses of organic compounds. The same industrial list also includes making perfumes, dyes, soaps and drugs.

mcqs.q: Acetic acid is obtained from:
mcqs.why: Acetic acid is obtained from vinegar, which is a natural source. It is an example of a useful organic compound that comes from a natural source rather than from petroleum or coal.

mcqs.q: The pharmaceutical chemist plays an important role in:
mcqs.why: The pharmaceutical chemist plays an important role in laboratory analysis, quality assurance and the production of new effective drugs. Quality assurance is therefore one of his named responsibilities in the notes.

mcqs.q: Besides laboratory analysis and quality assurance, the pharmaceutical chemist helps in:
options: The production of new effective drugs
mcqs.why: The pharmaceutical chemist's role covers laboratory analysis, quality assurance and the production of new effective drugs. Producing new effective drugs is the third part of his role as stated in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an industrial use of organic compounds?
mcqs.why: Making soaps is one of the industrial uses of organic compounds, along with making perfumes, dyes, plastics and drugs. The other options are not listed as uses of organic compounds in this lesson.

mcqs.q: Petrol, diesel and kerosene are all used as:
mcqs.why: Petrol, diesel and kerosene are used as fuel, and all of them are organic compounds. They are fractions obtained from petroleum and are among the most familiar fuel uses of organic compounds.

mcqs.q: In daily life, organic compounds are used as:
mcqs.why: In daily life organic compounds are used as food, as clothing, as houses (shelter), as fuel, as medicines and as raw materials. Food, clothing and medicines therefore all belong to the general uses listed in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Making perfumes and dyes is which kind of use of organic compounds?
mcqs.why: Making perfumes and making dyes are industrial uses of organic compounds, together with making soaps, plastics and drugs. They are carried out in industry rather than being simple daily-life uses like food or clothing.

mcqs.q: Organic compounds serve industry as:
mcqs.why: Organic compounds are used as raw materials, which is one of their general uses in daily life alongside food, clothing, shelter, fuel and medicines. Industry then converts such materials into perfumes, dyes, soaps, plastics and drugs.

lessons.title: Alkanes and Alkyl Radicals
lessons.notes_html:
Saturated and Unsaturated Hydrocarbons

TypeBondExample and General Formula
Saturated (alkanes)Single bonds between carbon atomsCnH2n+2, for example propane CH3CH2CH3
Unsaturated (alkenes)Double bond C=C between carbon atomsCnH2n
Unsaturated (alkynes)Triple bond C#C between carbon atomsCnH2n-2

Alkanes up to Decane

NameFormulaNameFormula
MethaneCH4HexaneC6H14
EthaneC2H6HeptaneC7H16
PropaneC3H8OctaneC8H18
ButaneC4H10NonaneC9H20
PentaneC5H12DecaneC10H22

Types of Formulae

  • Pentane: molecular formula C5H12, condensed formula CH3(CH2)3CH3, structural formula CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3.
  • Octane: molecular formula C8H18, condensed formula CH3(CH2)6CH3, structural formula CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3.

Alkyl Radicals

An alkyl radical is formed by removing one hydrogen atom from an alkane. Its general formula is CnH2n+1.

  • Methyl CH3- from methane CH4
  • Ethyl CH3CH2- from ethane C2H6
  • Propyl C3H7- from propane

mcqs.q: What is the general formula of alkanes?
mcqs.why: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with single bonds between carbon atoms, and their general formula is CnH2n+2. Propane, CH3CH2CH3, is given as an example of this family in the notes.

mcqs.q: Alkenes contain which bond between carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with a double bond C=C between carbon atoms, and their general formula is CnH2n. Alkynes, by contrast, contain a triple bond and follow CnH2n-2.

mcqs.q: The general formula CnH2n-2 belongs to:
mcqs.why: The general formula CnH2n-2 belongs to the alkynes, the unsaturated hydrocarbons with a triple bond between carbon atoms. Alkanes follow CnH2n+2 and alkenes follow CnH2n, so those options are wrong.

mcqs.q: What is the molecular formula of propane?
mcqs.why: Propane has the molecular formula C3H8, following the alkane general formula CnH2n+2 with n = 3. It is also written CH3CH2CH3 as the example of a saturated hydrocarbon in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Hexane has the molecular formula:
mcqs.why: Hexane has the formula C6H14, which fits the alkane series CnH2n+2 for six carbon atoms. In the same table, pentane is C5H12 and heptane is C7H16.

mcqs.q: The molecular formula of decane is:
mcqs.why: Decane, the tenth alkane in the table, has the molecular formula C10H22. It follows CnH2n+2 with n = 10, while nonane is C9H20 and octane is C8H18.

mcqs.q: The condensed formula of pentane is:
mcqs.why: Pentane's condensed formula is CH3(CH2)3CH3, and its structural formula is CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3. Its plain molecular formula is C5H12, which is a different type of formula from the condensed one asked for here.

mcqs.q: Octane has the molecular formula C8H18. Its condensed formula is:
mcqs.why: Octane's condensed formula is CH3(CH2)6CH3, matching its structural formula with eight carbon atoms in a row. CH3(CH2)3CH3 is instead the condensed formula of pentane, which has only five carbons.

mcqs.q: An alkyl radical is formed by:
options: Adding one hydrogen atom to an alkane
Removing one carbon atom from an alkane
Removing one hydrogen atom from an alkane
Adding a double bond to an alkane
mcqs.why: An alkyl radical is formed by removing one hydrogen atom from an alkane, and its general formula is CnH2n+1. For example, removing one hydrogen from methane CH4 gives the methyl radical CH3-.

mcqs.q: The ethyl radical CH3CH2- is obtained from:
mcqs.why: The ethyl radical CH3CH2- is formed from ethane C2H6 by removing one hydrogen atom. Similarly, methyl CH3- comes from methane and propyl C3H7- comes from propane.

lessons.title: Names of Simple Alkanes, Alkenes and Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
What is Nomenclature?

Nomenclature is the system of giving systematic names to compounds. By it, every compound has one accepted name.

Prefixes (Number of Carbons)

CarbonsPrefixCarbonsPrefix
1Meth6Hex
2Eth7Hept
3Prop8Oct
4But9Non
5Pent10Dec

Suffixes

  • For alkanes -ane: methane, ethane, propane...
  • For alkenes -ene: ethene, propene...
  • For alkynes -yne: ethyne, propyne...

Identifying the Name from the Formula

  • C2H4 — follows the pattern CnH2n, so it is an alkene: ethene
  • C3H6 — propene
  • C6H12 — hexene
  • C8H16 — octene
  • C3H4 — follows the pattern CnH2n-2, so it is an alkyne: propyne
  • C5H8 — pentyne, C7H12 — heptyne, C6H10 — hexyne

IUPAC Rules for Alkynes

  • Select the longest continuous chain containing the triple bond.
  • Number the chain from the end nearest the triple bond.
  • Name = prefix for the number of carbons + yne, for example ethyne, propyne.
  • If there are branches, their names and position numbers are written first.

mcqs.q: Nomenclature is:
options: The system of giving systematic names to compounds
The removal of hydrogen from alkanes
mcqs.why: Nomenclature is the system of giving systematic names to compounds, by which every compound has one accepted name. The prefixes for carbon numbers and the suffixes -ane, -ene and -yne are the tools of this system.

mcqs.q: The prefix for six carbon atoms is:
mcqs.why: The prefix for six carbon atoms is Hex, as in hexene and hexyne. Pent stands for five carbons, Hept for seven and Oct for eight, according to the prefix table in the lesson.

mcqs.q: The prefix 'Non' stands for how many carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: The prefix Non stands for nine carbon atoms. In the prefix table, Hept is seven, Oct is eight, Non is nine and Dec is ten.

mcqs.q: The suffix used for alkenes is:
mcqs.why: Alkenes take the suffix -ene, giving names such as ethene and propene. Alkanes end in -ane and alkynes end in -yne, so those suffixes belong to different families.

mcqs.q: Ethyne and propyne are names of:
mcqs.why: Ethyne and propyne are alkynes, named with the suffix -yne. Alkyne names are built from the prefix for the number of carbons plus -yne, following the IUPAC rules given in the lesson.

mcqs.q: C2H4 follows the pattern CnH2n, so it is the alkene named:
mcqs.why: C2H4 follows the pattern CnH2n, so it is an alkene, and with two carbons its name is ethene. Ethane would be C2H6 and ethyne would be C2H2, so neither of those fits the given formula.

mcqs.q: The alkene with formula C6H12 is named:
mcqs.why: C6H12 follows the alkene pattern CnH2n, and six carbons take the prefix Hex, giving hexene. Hexane would be the alkane C6H14 and hexyne would be the alkyne C6H10.

mcqs.q: C3H4 follows the pattern CnH2n-2, so it is:
mcqs.why: C3H4 follows the pattern CnH2n-2, so it is an alkyne, and with three carbons it is named propyne. Propene would be C3H6 and propane would be C3H8, so those options do not match.

mcqs.q: The alkyne C7H12 is named:
mcqs.why: C7H12 is an alkyne because it follows CnH2n-2, and seven carbons take the prefix Hept, giving heptyne. The lesson lists C7H12 — heptyne among its identification examples, along with pentyne and hexyne.

mcqs.q: According to the IUPAC rules for alkynes, the chain is numbered from:
options: The end nearest the triple bond
The end farthest from the triple bond
Either end, it does not matter
mcqs.why: For alkynes, the longest continuous chain containing the triple bond is selected and the chain is numbered from the end nearest the triple bond. The name is then the prefix for the number of carbons plus -yne, with any branches named first.

lessons.title: Introduction to Functional Groups
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Functional Group?

A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that gives a molecule its characteristic properties. Compounds are divided into separate families on the basis of their functional group.

Functional Groups Containing Carbon, Hydrogen and Oxygen

Functional GroupFormulaExample
Alcohol-OHCH3CH2OH
Ether-O-CH3OCH3
Aldehyde-CHOCH3CHO
Ketone-CO-CH3-CO-CH3
Carboxylic acid-COOHCH3-COOH
Ester-COOR—

Identification Examples

  • In CH3-CHO there is -CHO, the aldehyde group.
  • In CH3-CH2-CH2-OH there is -OH, the alcohol group.
  • In CH3-CO-CH3 there is -CO-, the ketone group.
  • In CH3-COOH there is -COOH, the carboxylic acid group.
  • In CH2=CH-CH3 there is C=C, the alkene double bond.

Functional Group and Property

If blue litmus paper dipped in a solution turns red, the solution is acidic, so it has the carboxylic acid group -COOH, which gives the acidic character. Remember that -COOH is used for carboxylic acids.

mcqs.q: A functional group is:
options: An atom or group of atoms that gives a molecule its characteristic properties
A long chain of carbon atoms only
A group of identical molecules in a sample
The part of a molecule that never reacts
mcqs.why: A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that gives a molecule its characteristic properties. Compounds are divided into separate families on the basis of their functional group, such as alcohols, aldehydes and carboxylic acids.

mcqs.q: The functional group of an alcohol is:
mcqs.why: Alcohols contain the -OH functional group, as in the example CH3CH2OH. The -CHO group belongs to aldehydes and -COOH to carboxylic acids, so those options name different families.

mcqs.q: CH3OCH3 contains the ether group, which is:
mcqs.why: The ether functional group is -O-, and CH3OCH3 is the example given for an ether. The -CO- group belongs to ketones and -CHO to aldehydes, so they are not the ether group.

mcqs.q: The aldehyde group -CHO is present in:
mcqs.why: CH3CHO contains -CHO, the aldehyde group, as shown in the identification examples. CH3CH2OH is an alcohol, CH3-CO-CH3 is a ketone and CH3-COOH is a carboxylic acid.

mcqs.q: In CH3-CO-CH3, the functional group -CO- shows that the compound is a:
mcqs.why: CH3-CO-CH3 contains the -CO- group, which is the ketone functional group. The lesson's identification examples use exactly this compound to illustrate how a functional group decides the family of a compound.

mcqs.q: The carboxylic acid group is written as:
mcqs.why: The carboxylic acid group is -COOH, as in CH3-COOH. The lesson stresses remembering that -COOH is used for carboxylic acids, and it is this group that gives the acidic character.

mcqs.q: The functional group of an ester is:
mcqs.why: Esters contain the -COOR functional group, listed among the groups containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. The other options are the alcohol (-OH), ketone (-CO-) and aldehyde (-CHO) groups.

mcqs.q: In CH3-CH2-CH2-OH, the functional group present is:
mcqs.why: CH3-CH2-CH2-OH contains -OH, the alcohol group, as the identification examples show. A compound is placed in the alcohol family because this group gives it its characteristic properties.

mcqs.q: The compound CH2=CH-CH3 is identified by the presence of:
mcqs.why: CH2=CH-CH3 contains C=C, the alkene double bond, which is its identifying functional feature. It has no -OH or -COOH group and no triple bond, so the double bond is the correct identification.

mcqs.q: If blue litmus paper dipped in a solution turns red, the solution is acidic and contains:
mcqs.why: Blue litmus turning red shows the solution is acidic, so it has the carboxylic acid group -COOH, which gives the acidic character. Alcohol, ether and ketone groups do not give this acidic behaviour.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates
lessons.notes_html:
What are carbohydrates?

Carbohydrates are organic compounds containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with the general formula Cx(H2O)y. They contain an aldehyde group -CHO or a ketone group >C=O along with many hydroxyl groups -OH. Examples: glucose, fructose, starch, cellulose.

Types of carbohydrates

TypeDefinitionExample
MonosaccharidesSimple sugars, cannot be simplified further on hydrolysisGlucose, fructose
OligosaccharidesGive 2 to 10 monosaccharides on hydrolysisSucrose, lactose
PolysaccharidesGive more than 10 monosaccharides on hydrolysisStarch, cellulose, glycogen
  • Glucose is an aldose because it contains an aldehyde group.
  • Lactose is called milk sugar.
  • Starch gives glucose on hydrolysis.
  • Cotton contains about 95 percent cellulose.

Sources

  • Monosaccharides: in grapes, honey and guava
  • Oligosaccharides: in sugarcane, sugar beet, milk, wheat and vegetables
  • Polysaccharides: in the cell walls of all land plants, in cotton, in cereal foods and in potato

Uses

  • They are a source of energy for survival.
  • They sustain the structure of plants.
  • They are a storage of energy in the form of starch and glucose.
  • They keep blood sugar levels in check.
  • Sucrose is used as a food additive.
  • Cellulose gives food its bulk and fibre and promotes peristalsis in the intestine.
  • Cellulose is a raw material in textiles and paper; starch is used in the production of ethanol and in laundries.

mcqs.q: The general formula of carbohydrates is:
mcqs.why: Carbohydrates are organic compounds containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with the general formula Cx(H2O)y. They also contain an aldehyde group -CHO or a ketone group >C=O along with many hydroxyl groups -OH.

mcqs.q: Besides many hydroxyl groups -OH, carbohydrates contain:
options: An aldehyde group -CHO or a ketone group >C=O
mcqs.why: Carbohydrates contain an aldehyde group -CHO or a ketone group >C=O along with many hydroxyl groups -OH. Glucose, fructose, starch and cellulose are the examples of carbohydrates given in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Monosaccharides are simple sugars that:
options: Give more than 10 units on hydrolysis
Cannot be simplified further on hydrolysis
mcqs.why: Monosaccharides are simple sugars that cannot be simplified further on hydrolysis, and glucose and fructose are examples. Polysaccharides, in contrast, give more than 10 monosaccharides on hydrolysis.

mcqs.q: Oligosaccharides give, on hydrolysis:
mcqs.why: Oligosaccharides give 2 to 10 monosaccharides on hydrolysis, and sucrose and lactose are examples. This places them between monosaccharides, which cannot be simplified further, and polysaccharides, which give more than 10 units.

mcqs.q: Starch, cellulose and glycogen are examples of:
mcqs.why: Starch, cellulose and glycogen are polysaccharides, which give more than 10 monosaccharides on hydrolysis. They are found in the cell walls of land plants, in cotton, in cereal foods and in potato.

mcqs.q: Glucose is called an aldose because it contains:
mcqs.why: Glucose is an aldose because it contains an aldehyde group. This fits the definition of carbohydrates, which carry either an aldehyde group -CHO or a ketone group >C=O with many -OH groups.

mcqs.q: Lactose is commonly called:
mcqs.why: Lactose is called milk sugar, and it is an oligosaccharide that gives 2 to 10 monosaccharides on hydrolysis. Oligosaccharides are found in sources such as sugarcane, sugar beet, milk, wheat and vegetables.

mcqs.q: On hydrolysis, starch gives:
mcqs.why: Starch gives glucose on hydrolysis, since starch is a polysaccharide built from many glucose units. Starch is also a storage of energy and is used in the production of ethanol and in laundries.

mcqs.q: Cotton contains about what percentage of cellulose?
mcqs.why: Cotton contains about 95 percent cellulose, making it a rich source of this polysaccharide. Cellulose also sustains the structure of plants and is a raw material in textiles and paper.

mcqs.q: Monosaccharides are found in:
mcqs.why: Monosaccharides are found in grapes, honey and guava, according to the sources listed in the lesson. Polysaccharides, by comparison, occur in the cell walls of all land plants, cotton, cereal foods and potato.

lessons.title: Proteins
lessons.notes_html:
What are proteins?

Proteins are polymers of amino acids, joined to one another by peptide bonds. One protein may contain from 60 to 6000 amino acid molecules. A protein is a hetero polymer and a polyamide.

Amino acids

Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. They have an amino group -NH2 and a carboxyl group -COOH on the same carbon atom. General structure: a central carbon atom joined to H, -NH2, -COOH and a side chain R.

Peptide bond

A peptide bond is the covalent bond that joins two amino acids to each other, between the carboxyl group of one and the amino group of the other.

TypeNumber of amino acids
Dipeptide2
Tripeptide3
PolypeptideMany

Functions of proteins

  • Proteins are the building blocks of the body.
  • As enzymes, they catalyze biological reactions.
  • As haemoglobin, they carry oxygen.

mcqs.q: Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined to one another by:
mcqs.why: Proteins are polymers of amino acids, joined to one another by peptide bonds. A protein is a hetero polymer and a polyamide, and one protein may contain from 60 to 6000 amino acid molecules.

mcqs.q: One protein molecule may contain how many amino acid molecules?
mcqs.why: One protein may contain from 60 to 6000 amino acid molecules joined by peptide bonds. This wide range shows why proteins are large polymer molecules built from amino acid building blocks.

mcqs.q: A protein is described as a hetero polymer and a:
mcqs.why: A protein is a hetero polymer and a polyamide, because it is built from amino acids linked by peptide (amide) bonds. It is not a polysaccharide like starch or a polyester, which belong to other classes of compounds.

mcqs.q: Amino acids are called the building blocks of:
mcqs.why: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, since proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Each amino acid carries an amino group -NH2 and a carboxyl group -COOH on the same carbon atom.

mcqs.q: An amino acid has which two groups on the same carbon atom?
mcqs.why: Amino acids have an amino group -NH2 and a carboxyl group -COOH on the same carbon atom. In the general structure, the central carbon is joined to H, -NH2, -COOH and a side chain R.

mcqs.q: In the general structure of an amino acid, the central carbon atom is joined to:
options: H, -NH2, -COOH and a side chain R
A phosphate group and a base
mcqs.why: The general structure of an amino acid has a central carbon atom joined to H, -NH2, -COOH and a side chain R. The side chain R is the part that differs from one amino acid to another.

mcqs.q: A peptide bond joins two amino acids between:
options: The carboxyl group of one and the amino group of the other
mcqs.why: A peptide bond is the covalent bond that joins two amino acids, between the carboxyl group of one and the amino group of the other. Chains built this way form dipeptides, tripeptides and polypeptides.

mcqs.q: A dipeptide contains how many amino acids?
mcqs.why: A dipeptide contains 2 amino acids joined by a peptide bond. A tripeptide contains 3, while a polypeptide contains many amino acids, as shown in the classification table.

mcqs.q: A chain of many amino acids is called a:
mcqs.why: A polypeptide contains many amino acids, unlike a dipeptide with 2 and a tripeptide with 3. Proteins themselves are large polypeptide-type polymers and may contain 60 to 6000 amino acid molecules.

mcqs.q: As haemoglobin, proteins perform which function?
mcqs.why: As haemoglobin, proteins carry oxygen, which is one of their listed functions. Proteins also act as the building blocks of the body and, as enzymes, catalyze biological reactions.

lessons.title: Lipids
lessons.notes_html:
What are lipids?

Lipids include fats and oils. Both are esters of fatty acids and glycerol.

Difference between fats and oils

FatsOils
Are solids at room temperatureAre liquids at room temperature
Increase the cholesterol level in the bodyAre generally obtained from plants
Examples: butter, gheeExamples: sunflower oil, olive oil

Sources

  • From animals: marine animals like salmon and whales, butter, ghee and cheese
  • From plants: sunflower, coconut, ground nuts, corn, cotton seed and olive

Uses

  • Lipids act as transporters of fatty acids in the body.
  • They are transporters of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
  • Some lipids reduce the cholesterol level.
  • Fats and oils are used for cooking and frying food.
  • They are used in detergents, soaps, cosmetics, polishes and paints.
  • They activate the enzymes.
  • Butter and ghee are used in bakery products and sweets.

mcqs.q: Lipids include fats and oils, and both are esters of:
mcqs.why: Lipids include fats and oils, and both are esters of fatty acids and glycerol. Fats and oils differ mainly in their physical state: fats are solids at room temperature while oils are liquids.

mcqs.q: At room temperature, fats are:
mcqs.why: Fats are solids at room temperature, with butter and ghee as examples. Oils such as sunflower oil and olive oil are liquids at room temperature, which is the key difference between the two.

mcqs.q: Oils are generally obtained from:
mcqs.why: Oils are generally obtained from plants, and sunflower oil and olive oil are the examples given. Fats like butter and ghee, by contrast, are solids and tend to increase the cholesterol level in the body.

mcqs.q: Compared with oils, fats tend to:
options: Have no effect on the body
Increase the cholesterol level in the body
mcqs.why: Fats increase the cholesterol level in the body, whereas some lipids reduce the cholesterol level. This difference is part of the comparison between fats and oils given in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Butter and ghee are examples of:
mcqs.why: Butter and ghee are examples of fats, which are solids at room temperature. They are obtained from animals and are used in bakery products and sweets, as well as for cooking and frying.

mcqs.q: Sunflower oil and olive oil are obtained from which source?
mcqs.why: Sunflower oil and olive oil are plant products, since plant sources of lipids include sunflower, coconut, ground nuts, corn, cotton seed and olive. Animal sources include marine animals like salmon and whales, butter, ghee and cheese.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an animal source of lipids?
mcqs.why: Marine animals like salmon and whales are animal sources of lipids, along with butter, ghee and cheese. Coconut, ground nuts and corn are all listed as plant sources instead.

mcqs.q: Lipids act as transporters of the fat-soluble vitamins:
mcqs.why: Lipids are transporters of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K in the body. They also act as transporters of fatty acids and activate the enzymes, which are further uses listed in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Fats and oils are used in making:
options: Detergents, soaps, cosmetics, polishes and paints
mcqs.why: Fats and oils are used in detergents, soaps, cosmetics, polishes and paints. They are also used for cooking and frying food, and butter and ghee are used in bakery products and sweets.

mcqs.q: One use of lipids in the body is that they:
mcqs.why: Lipids activate the enzymes, which is one of their uses listed in the lesson. They also transport fatty acids and the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, while carrying oxygen is the job of the protein haemoglobin.

lessons.title: Nucleic Acids
lessons.notes_html:
What are nucleic acids?

Nucleic acids are macromolecules formed by the polymerization of nucleotides. Each nucleotide is composed of a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. They store and transmit hereditary information.

DNA

  • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the store house of information.
  • It stores and transmits hereditary information from parents to children.
  • It encodes genetic information and transfers it from generation to generation.
  • Present in the nuclei of cells, it carries the information for making organs like heart, liver, eyes, kidneys, legs and head.
  • DNA is the most important thing in any living organism.

RNA

  • RNA (ribonucleic acid) receives the information obtained from DNA.
  • It decodes, reads and uses the information.
DNARNA
It is the store house of informationIt puts the information to use
It encodes genetic information and transfers it from generation to generationIt receives, decodes and reads the information

mcqs.q: Nucleic acids are macromolecules formed by the polymerization of:
mcqs.why: Nucleic acids are macromolecules formed by the polymerization of nucleotides. Each nucleotide is composed of a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base, and together they store and transmit hereditary information.

mcqs.q: Each nucleotide is composed of:
options: A pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base
An amino group and a carboxyl group
mcqs.why: Each nucleotide is composed of a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. Nucleic acids are built by joining many such nucleotides together through polymerization.

mcqs.q: The main role of nucleic acids is to:
mcqs.why: Nucleic acids store and transmit hereditary information, which is their defining role in living organisms. DNA is the store house of this information, while RNA receives and uses it.

mcqs.q: DNA stands for:
mcqs.why: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid, and it is described as the store house of information. It stores and transmits hereditary information from parents to children and is present in the nuclei of cells.

mcqs.q: DNA is described in the lesson as:
mcqs.why: DNA is the store house of information and is called the most important thing in any living organism. It encodes genetic information and transfers it from generation to generation.

mcqs.q: DNA is present in which part of the cell?
mcqs.why: DNA is present in the nuclei of cells, where it carries the information for making organs like heart, liver, eyes, kidneys, legs and head. This information is passed from parents to children.

mcqs.q: DNA transfers hereditary information:
mcqs.why: DNA encodes genetic information and transfers it from generation to generation, storing and transmitting hereditary information from parents to children. RNA then receives the information obtained from DNA.

mcqs.q: RNA stands for:
mcqs.why: RNA stands for ribonucleic acid, and it receives the information obtained from DNA. While DNA stores the information, RNA decodes, reads and uses it.

mcqs.q: The work of RNA is to:
options: Receive the information obtained from DNA
mcqs.why: RNA receives the information obtained from DNA, and then decodes, reads and uses that information. DNA, in contrast, is the store house that encodes and transfers the information between generations.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly contrasts DNA and RNA?
options: DNA puts information to use; RNA stores it
DNA is the store house of information; RNA puts the information to use
mcqs.why: DNA is the store house of information, while RNA puts the information to use by receiving, decoding and reading it. This contrast is the summary of the comparison table given in the lesson.

lessons.title: Vitamins
lessons.notes_html:
What are vitamins?

Vitamins are accessory growth factors which are needed in small amounts for the growth and health of the body.

Types of vitamins

TypeVitaminsProperty
Fat-solubleA, D, E, KStored in the body; excess can cause harm
Water-solubleB complex, CNot stored in the body; excess does not cause harm

Role of each vitamin

  • Vitamin A: necessary for sight
  • Vitamin D: for bones; helps in the use of calcium and phosphorus
  • Vitamin E: for protection of cells
  • Vitamin K: for clotting of blood
  • Vitamin B complex: for energy and nerves
  • Vitamin C: for skin and immunity

Vitamin D in particular

Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin. It is necessary to keep bones and teeth strong. Its deficiency causes rickets in children and weakness of bones in adults. Excess of vitamin D in the body causes calcification and pain in bones.

Deficiency diseases and harms of excess

VitaminDeficiencyExcess
AWeakness of sightIrritation and headache
DRicketsCalcification and pain in bones
B complexNerve and energy problems—
CScurvy—
E—Fatigue and headache
KDelay in clotting of bloodLiver and kidney diseases

mcqs.q: Vitamins are accessory growth factors that are needed:
options: In small amounts for the growth and health of the body
mcqs.why: Vitamins are accessory growth factors which are needed in small amounts for the growth and health of the body. They are divided into fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K and water-soluble vitamins B complex and C.

mcqs.q: The fat-soluble vitamins are:
mcqs.why: The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K, and they are stored in the body, so an excess of them can cause harm. The water-soluble vitamins, B complex and C, are not stored in the body.

mcqs.q: Water-soluble vitamins B complex and C are:
options: Not stored in the body, and excess does not cause harm
Stored in the body, and excess causes harm
mcqs.why: Water-soluble vitamins B complex and C are not stored in the body, and their excess does not cause harm. This is the opposite of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, which are stored and can harm in excess.

mcqs.q: Vitamin A is necessary for:
mcqs.why: Vitamin A is necessary for sight, and its deficiency causes weakness of sight, while its excess causes irritation and headache. Vitamin K is the one needed for clotting of blood, and vitamin E protects cells.

mcqs.q: Vitamin D helps the body in the use of:
mcqs.why: Vitamin D is for bones and helps in the use of calcium and phosphorus, keeping bones and teeth strong. Its deficiency causes rickets in children and weakness of bones in adults.

mcqs.q: Deficiency of vitamin D in children causes:
mcqs.why: Deficiency of vitamin D causes rickets in children and weakness of bones in adults, because vitamin D keeps bones and teeth strong. Scurvy is instead caused by deficiency of vitamin C.

mcqs.q: Vitamin K is needed for:
mcqs.why: Vitamin K is needed for clotting of blood, and its deficiency causes delay in clotting of blood. Its excess, on the other hand, causes liver and kidney diseases.

mcqs.q: Deficiency of vitamin C causes:
mcqs.why: Deficiency of vitamin C causes scurvy, and vitamin C is needed for skin and immunity. It is a water-soluble vitamin, so it is not stored in the body and its excess does not cause harm.

mcqs.q: Vitamin B complex is important for:
mcqs.why: Vitamin B complex is important for energy and nerves, and its deficiency leads to nerve and energy problems. It is a water-soluble vitamin group, unlike the fat-soluble A, D, E and K.

mcqs.q: Excess of vitamin D in the body causes:
