mcqs.why: Excess of vitamin D in the body causes calcification and pain in bones, because vitamin D is fat-soluble and stored in the body. Excess of vitamin A causes irritation and headache, and excess of vitamin E causes fatigue and headache.

lessons.title: Composition of the Atmosphere
lessons.notes_html:
What is the Atmosphere?

The atmosphere is the blanket of gases around the earth that covers the earth and is held to the earth by gravity. It is necessary for life and controls weather, air and temperature.

Composition of the Atmosphere

GasPercentage
Nitrogen78.09 percent
Oxygen20.95 percent
Argon0.93 percent
Carbon dioxide0.03 percent

Besides these there are water vapour, ozone, helium, methane and other small gases. Around 80 percent of the mass of the atmosphere is in the troposphere.

mcqs.q: What is the atmosphere?
options: The blanket of gases around the Earth, held to it by gravity
A layer of water covering the oceans
A ring of dust circling the Earth
The layer of clouds above the mountains
mcqs.why: The notes define the atmosphere as the blanket of gases around the Earth that covers the Earth and is held to it by gravity. It is a gaseous envelope, not a layer of water, dust or clouds.

mcqs.q: Besides being necessary for life, the atmosphere also controls which of the following?
mcqs.why: According to the notes, the atmosphere is necessary for life and it controls weather, air and temperature. It does not control the Moon, the oceans' depth or the Earth's rotation.

mcqs.q: Which gas makes up the largest share of the atmosphere?
mcqs.why: Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere, making up 78.09 percent of it. This is far more than oxygen, argon or carbon dioxide, so nitrogen is the correct answer.

mcqs.q: What is the percentage of nitrogen in the atmosphere?
mcqs.why: The composition table in the notes gives nitrogen as 78.09 percent of the atmosphere. The other values belong to oxygen (20.95), argon (0.93) and carbon dioxide (0.03) percent.

mcqs.q: What percentage of the atmosphere is oxygen?
mcqs.why: The notes state that oxygen makes up 20.95 percent of the atmosphere, the second largest share after nitrogen. The figures 78.09 and 0.93 percent belong to nitrogen and argon respectively.

mcqs.q: Argon accounts for what percentage of the atmosphere?
mcqs.why: The composition table lists argon at 0.93 percent of the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide is only 0.03 percent, while oxygen is 20.95 percent, so 0.93 percent is correct for argon.

mcqs.q: What is the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
mcqs.why: The notes give carbon dioxide as just 0.03 percent of the atmosphere, the smallest share among the main gases listed. Argon, at 0.93 percent, is still much more abundant than carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is also present in the atmosphere besides nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide?
mcqs.why: The notes say that besides the main gases there are water vapour, ozone, helium, methane and other small gases in the atmosphere. Of the options given, only helium is named in the notes.

mcqs.q: Around 80 percent of the mass of the atmosphere is found in which layer?
mcqs.why: The notes state that around 80 percent of the mass of the atmosphere is in the troposphere, the lowest layer. Most of the air is concentrated near the Earth's surface, not in the higher layers.

mcqs.q: Which gas has the second highest percentage in the atmosphere?
mcqs.why: Oxygen, at 20.95 percent, is the second most abundant gas after nitrogen at 78.09 percent. Argon (0.93 percent) and carbon dioxide (0.03 percent) are present in much smaller amounts.

lessons.title: Layers of the Atmosphere
lessons.notes_html:
Layers of the Atmosphere

There are 5 main layers of the atmosphere, from the earth upward in this order: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.

Troposphere

  • It is the lowest layer, from the earth's surface to about 11 to 12 kilometres.
  • It contains about 75 to 80 percent of the mass of the atmosphere.
  • Weather occurs in this layer and almost all aeroplanes pass through this layer.
  • The temperature falls with height, from 15 C to -56 C.
  • There is much air movement and an active weather system in it.

Stratosphere

  • It is the second layer, from 12 to about 50 to 55 kilometres.
  • It contains the ozone layer, which protects from ultraviolet radiation.
  • The temperature rises with height, because ozone absorbs radiation from the sun and gives heat.
  • Air movement is low and aeroplanes do not go in this layer.

Other Layers and Boundaries

  • The boundary separating the troposphere and the stratosphere is called the tropo-pause.
  • The mesosphere is above the stratosphere.
  • The thermosphere is the second highest layer of the earth's atmosphere; the highest is the exosphere.
  • Ozone gas is found in the stratosphere.
FeatureTroposphereStratosphere
Height0 to about 12 km12 to 50-55 km
Temperature with heightFalls (15 to -56 C)Rises
Special featureWeather and aeroplanesOzone layer
Air movementMuchLow

mcqs.q: How many main layers does the atmosphere have?
mcqs.why: The notes state that there are 5 main layers of the atmosphere. In order from the Earth upward they are the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct order of the atmospheric layers from the Earth upward?
mcqs.why: The notes list the layers from the Earth upward as troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere. Any other order mixes up the positions of the layers.

mcqs.q: Which is the lowest layer of the atmosphere?
mcqs.why: The troposphere is the lowest layer, extending from the Earth's surface upward. The stratosphere lies above it, and the mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere are higher still.

mcqs.q: The troposphere extends from the Earth's surface up to about what height?
mcqs.why: The notes say the troposphere reaches from the Earth's surface to about 11 to 12 kilometres. The 50 to 55 kilometre figure is the top of the stratosphere, not the troposphere.

mcqs.q: About how much of the mass of the atmosphere does the troposphere contain?
mcqs.why: According to the notes, the troposphere contains about 75 to 80 percent of the mass of the atmosphere. This is why most air and weather activity is concentrated in this lowest layer.

mcqs.q: What happens to the temperature as height increases in the troposphere?
options: It rises then suddenly drops to zero
mcqs.why: In the troposphere the temperature falls with height, from 15°C near the surface to -56°C at the top. This is the opposite behaviour to the stratosphere, where temperature rises with height.

mcqs.q: In which layer does weather occur and through which do almost all aeroplanes pass?
mcqs.why: The notes state that weather occurs in the troposphere and almost all aeroplanes pass through this layer. The stratosphere, by contrast, has low air movement and aeroplanes do not go in it.

mcqs.q: The boundary separating the troposphere and the stratosphere is called the:
mcqs.why: The notes name the boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere as the tropo-pause. The ozone layer is a region inside the stratosphere, not a boundary between layers.

mcqs.q: The stratosphere extends from about 12 kilometres up to about:
mcqs.why: The notes give the stratosphere's range as from 12 kilometres to about 50 to 55 kilometres. It is the second layer, sitting directly above the troposphere.

mcqs.q: Why does the temperature rise with height in the stratosphere?
options: Because there is much air movement
Because ozone absorbs radiation from the Sun and gives heat
mcqs.why: The notes explain that the temperature rises with height in the stratosphere because ozone absorbs radiation from the Sun and gives out heat. Air movement there is low, and weather and aeroplanes belong to the troposphere.

lessons.title: Pollutants
lessons.notes_html:
Primary and Secondary Pollutants

  • Primary pollutants come directly from sources, for example CO2 from vehicles and SO2 from factories.
  • Secondary pollutants are formed in the atmosphere by chemical reactions of primary pollutants, for example acid rain and ozone.

Major Air Pollutants and Their Sources

PollutantSource
Carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide, oxides of nitrogenVehicles and factories
Smoke and dustBurning of fuel
Pesticides and fertilizer particlesLand
Ozone and acid rainSecondary reactions

Effects on Human Health

  • Air pollutants affect the respiratory systems of humans and animals.
  • Acid rain and smoke damage the eyes and lungs.
  • Breathing polluted air can cause cough, asthma, lung diseases and allergy.
  • CO2 and other greenhouse gases cause global warming.

mcqs.q: What are primary pollutants?
options: Pollutants that come directly from sources
Pollutants formed by reactions in the air
mcqs.why: Primary pollutants come directly from sources, such as CO2 from vehicles and SO2 from factories. Pollutants formed later by chemical reactions in the atmosphere are secondary pollutants, not primary ones.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of a primary pollutant given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give SO2 from factories (and CO2 from vehicles) as examples of primary pollutants because they come directly from a source. Acid rain and ozone are secondary pollutants formed by reactions in the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: How are secondary pollutants formed?
options: They are produced inside factories only
They are released directly by vehicles
They are formed in the atmosphere by chemical reactions of primary pollutants
They wash off the land into rivers
mcqs.why: Secondary pollutants are formed in the atmosphere by chemical reactions of primary pollutants, as the notes state. Acid rain and ozone are the examples given of such pollutants.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a secondary pollutant?
mcqs.why: Acid rain is listed in the notes as a secondary pollutant, formed by reactions in the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide released directly from vehicles and factories are primary pollutants.

mcqs.q: Carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen mainly come from:
mcqs.why: The pollutant table in the notes gives vehicles and factories as the source of carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. Pesticides and fertilizer particles, by contrast, come from the land.

mcqs.q: Smoke and dust in the air come from:
mcqs.why: According to the notes, smoke and dust are produced by the burning of fuel. Ozone and acid rain come from secondary reactions, while pesticide particles come from the land.

mcqs.q: Pesticides and fertilizer particles that pollute the air come from:
mcqs.why: The notes list the land as the source of pesticides and fertilizer particles in the air. Vehicles and factories are the sources of the gaseous pollutants such as CO2, SO2 and oxides of nitrogen.

mcqs.q: Air pollutants mainly affect which system of humans and animals?
mcqs.why: The notes state that air pollutants affect the respiratory systems of humans and animals. Breathing polluted air leads to problems such as cough, asthma, lung diseases and allergy.

mcqs.q: Acid rain and smoke damage which parts of the body?
mcqs.why: The notes say that acid rain and smoke damage the eyes and lungs. This fits with the wider point that air pollutants attack the respiratory system of humans and animals.

mcqs.q: Carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in the air cause:
mcqs.why: The notes state that CO2 and other greenhouse gases cause global warming by trapping heat. Ozone depletion and acid rain are separate pollution problems with different causes.

lessons.title: Acid Rain and Its Effects
lessons.notes_html:
What is Acid Rain and How is it Formed?

The cause of acid rain is sulphur dioxide SO2 and oxides of nitrogen NO2 from factories and vehicles. These gases combine with water vapour in the atmosphere to form acidic compounds and come down with the rain. It is a secondary pollutant problem.

Effects of Acid Rain

  • It affects the respiratory system.
  • It harms the aquatic ecology; the living organisms of lakes and rivers are affected.
  • It corrodes water pipelines, so heavy metals like iron, lead and copper seep into drinking water.
  • It damages stone and metal buildings and monuments.

mcqs.q: What is the main cause of acid rain?
options: Sulphur dioxide (SO2) and oxides of nitrogen (NO2)
mcqs.why: The notes state that the cause of acid rain is sulphur dioxide SO2 and oxides of nitrogen NO2 from factories and vehicles. These gases, not carbon dioxide or ozone, are responsible for acid rain.

mcqs.q: The gases that cause acid rain come mainly from:
mcqs.why: According to the notes, the sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen that cause acid rain come from factories and vehicles. These are the man-made sources named in the lesson.

mcqs.q: How is acid rain actually formed in the atmosphere?
options: Dust settles into rainwater on the ground
SO2 and NO2 combine with water vapour to form acidic compounds that come down with the rain
Sunlight turns ordinary rain into acid
mcqs.why: The notes explain that SO2 and oxides of nitrogen combine with water vapour in the atmosphere to form acidic compounds, which then come down with the rain. This is how acid rain is produced.

mcqs.q: Acid rain is an example of which type of pollutant problem?
mcqs.why: The notes describe acid rain as a secondary pollutant problem, because it is not released directly but forms in the atmosphere when gases react with water vapour. That is why it is classed as secondary.

mcqs.q: Which body system is affected by acid rain, as stated in the notes?
mcqs.why: The effects list in the notes begins by saying that acid rain affects the respiratory system. Like other air pollution, its health harm is centred on breathing and the lungs.

mcqs.q: How does acid rain harm aquatic ecology?
options: It affects the living organisms of lakes and rivers
It warms the water of lakes
mcqs.why: The notes state that acid rain harms the aquatic ecology because the living organisms of lakes and rivers are affected. The damage is to the life in the water, not to the water's temperature or saltiness.

mcqs.q: What does acid rain do to water pipelines?
mcqs.why: The notes say acid rain corrodes water pipelines. Because of this corrosion, heavy metals seep from the pipes into the drinking water, making the water unsafe.

mcqs.q: Which heavy metals seep into drinking water when acid rain corrodes pipelines?
mcqs.why: The notes name iron, lead and copper as the heavy metals that seep into drinking water through corroded pipelines. These metals make the drinking water harmful for people.

mcqs.q: The heavy metals released by corroded pipelines end up in:
mcqs.why: According to the notes, acid rain corrodes water pipelines so that heavy metals like iron, lead and copper seep into drinking water. The danger is therefore in the water people drink.

mcqs.q: Besides pipelines and living things, what else does acid rain damage?
options: Roads and bridges made of wood
Stone and metal buildings and monuments
mcqs.why: The notes state that acid rain damages stone and metal buildings and monuments. This is one of its well-known effects on property, along with harm to health, aquatic life and pipelines.

lessons.title: Ozone Depletion and Its Effects
lessons.notes_html:
Ozone Layer

Ozone O3 is a gas which is found in the stratosphere. The ozone layer absorbs the harmful ultraviolet radiation of the sun and protects life on earth.

Formation of Ozone

In the stratosphere, ozone is formed from oxygen by the action of the sun's radiation and at the same time it also keeps breaking down; this natural balance maintains the ozone layer.

Ozone Depletion

  • Man-made chemicals, especially the gases used in refrigerators and air conditioners, break down ozone.
  • As ozone decreases, more ultraviolet radiation reaches the earth.

Effects

  • Ultraviolet radiation damages the eyes and lungs.
  • It is harmful for the skin and other living organisms.
  • Therefore protection of the ozone layer is necessary for the protection of life.

mcqs.q: What is the chemical formula of ozone?
mcqs.why: The notes write ozone as O3, a form of oxygen with three atoms. O2 is ordinary oxygen gas, while CO2 and H2O are carbon dioxide and water.

mcqs.q: In which layer of the atmosphere is ozone found?
mcqs.why: The notes state that ozone O3 is a gas found in the stratosphere, where it forms the ozone layer. It is this layer that absorbs the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.

mcqs.q: What does the ozone layer do for life on Earth?
options: It absorbs the harmful ultraviolet radiation of the Sun and protects life on Earth
mcqs.why: The notes say the ozone layer absorbs the harmful ultraviolet radiation of the Sun and protects life on Earth. Without this protection, much more damaging radiation would reach the surface.

mcqs.q: How is ozone formed in the stratosphere?
options: From carbon dioxide by plant action
From oxygen by the action of the Sun's radiation
mcqs.why: The notes explain that in the stratosphere ozone is formed from oxygen by the action of the Sun's radiation. At the same time ozone keeps breaking down, and this balance maintains the layer.

mcqs.q: What maintains the ozone layer in the stratosphere?
options: The natural balance between ozone being formed and ozone breaking down
The constant release of ozone from factories
mcqs.why: According to the notes, ozone is formed from oxygen by the Sun's radiation and at the same time keeps breaking down; this natural balance maintains the ozone layer. Human chemicals disturb this balance.

mcqs.q: What breaks down the ozone layer?
options: Man-made chemicals, especially the gases used in refrigerators and air conditioners
mcqs.why: The notes state that man-made chemicals, especially the gases used in refrigerators and air conditioners, break down ozone. This human-caused loss of ozone is called ozone depletion.

mcqs.q: As ozone decreases, what happens at the Earth's surface?
options: Less ultraviolet radiation reaches the Earth
The Earth becomes colder at once
More ultraviolet radiation reaches the Earth
mcqs.why: The notes explain that as ozone decreases, more ultraviolet radiation reaches the Earth, because there is less ozone to absorb it. This increase in radiation is what makes ozone depletion dangerous.

mcqs.q: Ultraviolet radiation that reaches the Earth in excess damages:
mcqs.why: The effects section of the notes states that ultraviolet radiation damages the eyes and lungs. It is also harmful for the skin and other living organisms.

mcqs.q: Why is protection of the ozone layer necessary, according to the notes?
options: For the protection of life on Earth
mcqs.why: The notes conclude that protection of the ozone layer is necessary for the protection of life, because the layer shields living things from harmful ultraviolet radiation. Letting it thin puts health and other organisms at risk.

mcqs.q: Which appliances' gases are especially blamed in the notes for breaking down ozone?
mcqs.why: The notes single out the gases used in refrigerators and air conditioners as the man-made chemicals that break down ozone. These are the examples given for ozone-depleting chemicals.

lessons.title: Greenhouse Effect
lessons.notes_html:
What is the Greenhouse Effect?

Greenhouse gases trap the sun's heat in the atmosphere, due to which the earth stays warm. This natural process is necessary for life, but with an increase in the gases it becomes greater.

Greenhouse Gases

  • Carbon dioxide CO2
  • Methane CH4
  • Nitrous oxide
  • Water vapour

Note: Oxygen is not a greenhouse gas.

Global Warming

  • With an increase in greenhouse gases, more heat is trapped, due to which the earth's temperature rises; this is called global warming.
  • Global warming is the continuous rise in the average temperature of the earth.
  • Results: the weather changes, ice melts, sea level rises and living organisms are badly affected.
  • The rise in CO2 concentration is a major cause of global warming, which increases by the burning of fuel.

mcqs.q: What do greenhouse gases do in the atmosphere?
options: They trap the Sun's heat in the atmosphere, due to which the Earth stays warm
They reflect all sunlight back to space
mcqs.why: The notes explain that greenhouse gases trap the Sun's heat in the atmosphere, due to which the Earth stays warm. This trapping of heat is the greenhouse effect.

mcqs.q: The greenhouse effect is best described as:
options: A process that cools the Earth
A natural process that is necessary for life, which becomes greater when greenhouse gases increase
A process found only in deserts
An artificial process caused only by factories
mcqs.why: The notes say the greenhouse effect is a natural process that is necessary for life, but with an increase in the gases it becomes greater. It is the excess, not the effect itself, that is the problem.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a greenhouse gas listed in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes list carbon dioxide CO2, methane CH4, nitrous oxide and water vapour as greenhouse gases. Oxygen is specifically noted as not being a greenhouse gas.

mcqs.q: What is the formula of methane, one of the greenhouse gases?
mcqs.why: Methane is written as CH4 in the notes' list of greenhouse gases. CO2 is carbon dioxide and O3 is ozone, so CH4 is the correct formula for methane.

mcqs.q: Which of these gases is named in the notes as a greenhouse gas?
mcqs.why: Nitrous oxide appears in the notes' list of greenhouse gases along with carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour. Oxygen, helium and argon are not in that list.

mcqs.q: Water vapour is classed in the notes as:
mcqs.why: Water vapour is included in the notes' list of greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and water vapour. It helps trap the Sun's heat in the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: Which gas is specifically stated in the notes to NOT be a greenhouse gas?
mcqs.why: The notes state clearly: 'Oxygen is not a greenhouse gas.' Methane, carbon dioxide and water vapour are all listed as greenhouse gases, so oxygen is the odd one out.

mcqs.q: What is global warming, as defined in the notes?
options: A rise in sea level only
The continuous rise in the average temperature of the Earth
The melting of ice in one season
A fall in the Earth's average temperature
mcqs.why: The notes define global warming as the continuous rise in the average temperature of the Earth, caused when increased greenhouse gases trap more heat. Ice melting and sea-level rise are its results, not its definition.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a result of global warming given in the notes?
options: Ice melts and sea level rises
mcqs.why: The notes list the results of global warming as: the weather changes, ice melts, sea level rises and living organisms are badly affected. Ice melting and sea-level rise are therefore correct results.

mcqs.q: A major cause of global warming is the rise in CO2 concentration, which increases by:
mcqs.why: The notes state that the rise in CO2 concentration is a major cause of global warming and that it increases by the burning of fuel. Burning fuel releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

lessons.title: Water
lessons.notes_html:
Presence of Water

  • About 70 percent of the Earth's surface is covered by water.
  • The percentage of fresh water is about 3 percent; most of the rest is the saline water of the oceans.
  • Our dependence on water is very great and it is very important to maintain its quality.

Composition of Water

A water molecule is made up of one atom of oxygen and two atoms of hydrogen, connected by covalent bonds: H2O. Because of the higher electronegativity of oxygen, the oxygen carries a partial negative charge and the hydrogens carry partial positive charges, so water is a polar molecule. Hydrogen bonding exists between water molecules.

Properties of Water

  • Water is colourless, odourless and tasteless.
  • Water is a polar solvent.

Why is Water a Universal Solvent?

Water is called the universal solvent, because it dissolves very many substances. The reason is that it is polar: it dissolves ionic compounds like NaCl and many molecular substances. The hydrogen bonding between water molecules also helps its solvent character. Water is important in both the environment and industry.

mcqs.q: About what percentage of the Earth's surface is covered by water?
mcqs.why: The notes state that about 70 percent of the Earth's surface is covered by water. Most of this water is the saline water of the oceans, and only a small part is fresh water.

mcqs.q: About what percentage of the Earth's water is fresh water?
mcqs.why: According to the notes, the percentage of fresh water is about 3 percent, while most of the rest is the saline water of the oceans. This is why maintaining the quality of fresh water is so important.

mcqs.q: Most of the water on Earth, apart from the small fresh-water share, is:
options: The saline water of the oceans
mcqs.why: The notes say that most of the water other than the roughly 3 percent fresh water is the saline water of the oceans. Rivers, groundwater and rain form only a very small part of the total.

mcqs.q: A water molecule is made up of:
options: Two oxygen atoms and one hydrogen atom
Two oxygen atoms and two hydrogen atoms
One oxygen atom and one hydrogen atom
One oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms
mcqs.why: The notes state that a water molecule is made up of one atom of oxygen and two atoms of hydrogen, giving the formula H2O. The two hydrogens are joined to the oxygen by covalent bonds.

mcqs.q: The atoms in a water molecule are connected by:
mcqs.why: According to the notes, the oxygen and hydrogen atoms in water are connected by covalent bonds, forming H2O. These bonds, together with oxygen's higher electronegativity, make water a polar molecule.

mcqs.q: Why does the oxygen atom in water carry a partial negative charge?
options: Because oxygen has a higher electronegativity than hydrogen
mcqs.why: The notes explain that because of the higher electronegativity of oxygen, the oxygen carries a partial negative charge and the hydrogens carry partial positive charges. This charge separation makes water a polar molecule.

mcqs.q: Water is described in the notes as what kind of molecule?
mcqs.why: The notes state that water is a polar molecule, because oxygen carries a partial negative charge and the hydrogens carry partial positive charges. This polarity is the key to water's solvent power.

mcqs.q: What type of bonding exists between separate water molecules?
mcqs.why: The notes state that hydrogen bonding exists between water molecules. This bonding also helps water's solvent character, alongside its polarity.

mcqs.q: Water is called the universal solvent because:
options: It covers most of the Earth
mcqs.why: The notes say water is called the universal solvent because it dissolves very many substances. The reason is its polarity: it dissolves ionic compounds like NaCl and many molecular substances.

mcqs.q: Which substance is given in the notes as an example of an ionic compound that water dissolves?
mcqs.why: The notes give NaCl as the example of an ionic compound that water dissolves because it is polar. Sand, oil and plastic are not named as substances water dissolves.

lessons.title: Soft and Hard Water
lessons.notes_html:
Soft and Hard Water

  • Soft water is water that forms lather easily with soap and contains very few salts of calcium and magnesium.
  • Hard water is water that does not form lather easily with soap, because it contains dissolved salts of calcium and magnesium — chlorides, sulphates and bicarbonates.

Types of Hardness

TypeCauseRemoved by Boiling?
Temporary hardnessCa(HCO3)2 and Mg(HCO3)2Yes
Permanent hardnessChlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium, such as MgSO4No

Methods to Remove Temporary Hardness

  • Boiling: on heating, the bicarbonate breaks down into insoluble carbonate which settles at the bottom.
  • Clark's method: adding slaked lime Ca(OH)2 converts the bicarbonate into carbonate which settles at the bottom.
  • Adding washing soda Na2CO3.

Methods to Remove Permanent Hardness

  • Adding washing soda Na2CO3: calcium and magnesium settle at the bottom as insoluble carbonates.
  • The sodium zeolite method: water is passed through zeolite which exchanges calcium and magnesium for sodium.
  • The ion exchange resin method.

Disadvantages of Hard Water

  • It does not form lather with soap, so soap is wasted and clothes are not cleaned.
  • It forms scale in boilers and pipes, which wastes energy and damages machines.
  • It affects the taste and cooking of food.
  • It can harm the skin and hair.

mcqs.q: What is soft water?
options: Water that forms lather easily with soap and contains very few salts of calcium and magnesium
Water that contains many dissolved salts
Water with no hydrogen in it
mcqs.why: The notes define soft water as water that forms lather easily with soap and contains very few salts of calcium and magnesium. Hard water is the opposite: it is loaded with these salts and lathers poorly.

mcqs.q: Why does hard water not form lather easily with soap?
options: Because it contains dissolved salts of calcium and magnesium
mcqs.why: The notes state that hard water does not form lather easily with soap because it contains dissolved salts of calcium and magnesium — chlorides, sulphates and bicarbonates. These salts are the cause of hardness.

mcqs.q: The dissolved salts that make water hard are the chlorides, sulphates and bicarbonates of:
mcqs.why: According to the notes, hard water contains dissolved salts of calcium and magnesium — their chlorides, sulphates and bicarbonates. Soft water contains very few of these salts.

mcqs.q: Temporary hardness of water is caused by:
mcqs.why: The hardness table in the notes shows temporary hardness is caused by Ca(HCO3)2 and Mg(HCO3)2, the bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium. MgSO4, a sulphate, causes permanent hardness instead.

mcqs.q: Can temporary hardness be removed by boiling?
mcqs.why: The notes state that temporary hardness can be removed by boiling: on heating, the bicarbonate breaks down into insoluble carbonate which settles at the bottom. Permanent hardness, by contrast, is not removed by boiling.

mcqs.q: What happens when water with temporary hardness is boiled?
options: The bicarbonate breaks down into insoluble carbonate which settles at the bottom
The bicarbonate changes into soluble salt
mcqs.why: The notes explain that on heating, the bicarbonate causing temporary hardness breaks down into insoluble carbonate which settles at the bottom. Removing this settled carbonate leaves the water soft.

mcqs.q: In Clark's method for removing temporary hardness, what is added to the water?
mcqs.why: Clark's method, as given in the notes, adds slaked lime Ca(OH)2, which converts the bicarbonate into carbonate that settles at the bottom. Washing soda is a different method used for hardness removal.

mcqs.q: Permanent hardness is caused by which salts?
options: Chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium, such as MgSO4
mcqs.why: The notes state that permanent hardness is caused by chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium, such as MgSO4. Unlike temporary hardness from bicarbonates, it cannot be removed by boiling.

mcqs.q: In the sodium zeolite method of softening water, the zeolite:
options: Exchanges calcium and magnesium for sodium
mcqs.why: The notes describe the sodium zeolite method: water is passed through zeolite which exchanges calcium and magnesium for sodium. Removing the calcium and magnesium makes the water soft.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of hard water given in the notes?
options: It improves the taste of food
It forms scale in boilers and pipes, which wastes energy and damages machines
mcqs.why: The notes list scale formation in boilers and pipes as a disadvantage of hard water, because it wastes energy and damages machines. Hard water also wastes soap and affects the taste and cooking of food.

lessons.title: Pollutants of Water
lessons.notes_html:
Definition of a Water Pollutant

A water pollutant is a substance that mixes in water and makes it unfit for drinking and other uses, for example chemical waste, sewage, pesticides, fertilizers and germs.

Industrial Pollutants

Industrial pollutants are the waste from factories:

  • Chemicals
  • Heavy metals like lead, mercury and cadmium
  • Oil, dyes and hot water

They mix into rivers and land, kill aquatic organisms, poison drinking water and pollute the land.

Domestic and Agricultural Pollutants

  • Domestic sewage, which contains germs
  • Pesticides and fertilizers which wash off the land and mix into water
  • They spoil the quality of water and spread diseases

Effects

  • Aquatic organisms die
  • Drinking water becomes poisonous
  • The land is polluted
  • Water-borne diseases spread

mcqs.q: What is a water pollutant?
options: A substance that mixes in water and makes it unfit for drinking and other uses
Any substance dissolved naturally in water
A gas found in the atmosphere
mcqs.why: The notes define a water pollutant as a substance that mixes in water and makes it unfit for drinking and other uses. Examples given are chemical waste, sewage, pesticides, fertilizers and germs.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is named in the notes as a water pollutant?
mcqs.why: Sewage is listed in the notes among water pollutants, together with chemical waste, pesticides, fertilizers and germs. Sand, oxygen and sunlight are not named as pollutants.

mcqs.q: Which heavy metals are named as industrial pollutants of water?
mcqs.why: The notes list heavy metals like lead, mercury and cadmium among industrial pollutants from factories. These poisonous metals mix into rivers and land and poison drinking water.

mcqs.q: Besides chemicals and heavy metals, industrial waste in water includes:
mcqs.why: The notes state that industrial pollutants include oil, dyes and hot water as well as chemicals and heavy metals. This factory waste kills aquatic organisms and poisons drinking water.

mcqs.q: Industrial pollutants harm the environment by:
options: Mixing into rivers and land, killing aquatic organisms and poisoning drinking water
mcqs.why: According to the notes, industrial pollutants mix into rivers and land, kill aquatic organisms, poison drinking water and pollute the land. They are a major cause of water pollution damage.

mcqs.q: Domestic sewage is dangerous as a water pollutant mainly because it:
mcqs.why: The notes point out that domestic sewage contains germs, which is why it spoils the quality of water and spreads diseases. Keeping sewage out of drinking water is essential for health.

mcqs.q: How do pesticides and fertilizers become water pollutants?
options: They are poured directly into wells by farmers
They are produced by factories in water
They wash off the land and mix into water
mcqs.why: The notes state that pesticides and fertilizers wash off the land and mix into water. Once in the water they spoil its quality and help spread diseases.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an effect of water pollution listed in the notes?
mcqs.why: The effects section of the notes states plainly that aquatic organisms die because of water pollution. Drinking water also becomes poisonous and the land is polluted.

mcqs.q: What happens to drinking water when pollutants mix into it, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes list 'drinking water becomes poisonous' as one of the effects of water pollution. Polluted water is unfit for drinking and other uses.

mcqs.q: Water pollution also leads to which health problem named in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state that water-borne diseases spread as a result of water pollution, along with aquatic organisms dying, drinking water becoming poisonous and the land being polluted.

lessons.title: Water-Borne Diseases
lessons.notes_html:
Names of the Diseases

The water-borne diseases are: diarrhoea, dysentery, cholera, cryptosporidium, fluorosis, hepatitis, hookworm, jaundice and typhoid.

Types by Cause

CauseDiseases
BacteriaCholera, typhoid
VirusHepatitis, polio; diarrhoea and dysentery are also caused by bacteria or viruses
WormsHookworm
Chemical (excess amount of fluoride)Fluorosis

How Do the Diseases Occur?

These diseases are caused by drinking or using polluted water. When sewage mixes into drinking water, germs enter the body.

Prevention

  • Drink clean water.
  • Boil or filter water.
  • Keep sewage away from drinking water.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is listed in the notes as a water-borne disease?
mcqs.why: Cholera heads the notes' list of water-borne diseases, which also includes diarrhoea, dysentery, typhoid, hepatitis and jaundice. Malaria, diabetes and asthma are not in that list.

mcqs.q: Cholera and typhoid are caused by:
mcqs.why: The cause table in the notes shows that cholera and typhoid are caused by bacteria. Hepatitis and polio are viral, hookworm is caused by worms, and fluorosis by excess fluoride.

mcqs.q: Hepatitis, a water-borne disease, is caused by:
mcqs.why: The notes place hepatitis under virus-caused diseases, together with polio. Cholera and typhoid, by contrast, are caused by bacteria.

mcqs.q: Which water-borne disease in the notes is caused by a virus, besides hepatitis?
mcqs.why: The notes state that hepatitis and polio are caused by viruses. Hookworm is caused by worms, fluorosis by excess fluoride, and typhoid by bacteria.

mcqs.q: Hookworm disease is caused by:
mcqs.why: The cause table in the notes lists hookworm under worms. It is the worm-caused entry among the water-borne diseases named in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Fluorosis is caused by:
options: An excess amount of fluoride (a chemical cause)
mcqs.why: The notes state that fluorosis is caused chemically, by an excess amount of fluoride. Unlike cholera or hepatitis, it is not caused by germs at all.

mcqs.q: Diarrhoea and dysentery, according to the notes, can be caused by:
mcqs.why: The notes state that diarrhoea and dysentery are also caused by bacteria or viruses, in addition to cholera and typhoid being bacterial and hepatitis being viral. Both kinds of germs can produce them.

mcqs.q: How do water-borne diseases mainly occur?
options: By drinking or using polluted water
mcqs.why: The notes explain that these diseases are caused by drinking or using polluted water. When sewage mixes into drinking water, germs enter the body and cause illness.

mcqs.q: When sewage mixes into drinking water, what happens?
mcqs.why: According to the notes, when sewage mixes into drinking water, germs enter the body and cause water-borne diseases. This is why sewage must be kept away from drinking water.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a prevention measure for water-borne diseases given in the notes?
options: Mix sewage away from homes only
mcqs.why: The prevention list in the notes includes drinking clean water, boiling or filtering water, and keeping sewage away from drinking water. Boiling or filtering water kills or removes the germs that cause these diseases.

lessons.title: Qualitative and Quantitative Analysis
lessons.notes_html:
What is Analytical Chemistry?

Analytical chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the instruments and methods to separate, identify and quantify matter. It is used in every type of chemistry: in organic, inorganic, physical and biochemistry, analytical methods are needed to identify samples and determine their quantity. Therefore it is a part of all types of chemistry.

Two Types

Qualitative AnalysisQuantitative Analysis
Tells which substances are present in a sampleTells in what quantity those substances are present
Example: chemical and flame testsExample: titrimetric, gravimetric and combustion analysis

First Step: Identification

The first step to quantify any sample is to identify it. Because first it is necessary to know which compounds are in the sample, and only then can their quantity be determined. If the compound is not identified, the method to measure its quantity cannot be chosen. Therefore first identification, then quantity.

Types of Qualitative Analysis

  • Organic qualitative analysis: deals with the identification of the presence of functional groups in compounds.
  • Inorganic qualitative analysis: identification of ions and elements, such as the flame test. The flame test of copper halide with bluish-green colour identifies the presence of halogen.
  • In qualitative analysis the sample may be solid, liquid, gas or a mixture.

mcqs.q: What does analytical chemistry deal with?
options: Only the synthesis of new compounds
The instruments and methods to separate, identify and quantify matter
The study of reaction rates only
mcqs.why: Analytical chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the instruments and methods used to separate, identify and quantify matter. It is not limited to synthesis, reaction rates or industrial manufacture; its focus is analysis of matter.

mcqs.q: Which of the following branches uses analytical methods to identify samples?
options: Organic, inorganic, physical chemistry and biochemistry
mcqs.why: The notes state that analytical methods are needed in organic, inorganic, physical chemistry and biochemistry to identify samples and determine their quantity. Therefore analytical chemistry is a part of all types of chemistry, not just one branch.

mcqs.q: What does qualitative analysis tell us about a sample?
options: In what quantity the substances are present
Which substances are present in the sample
The exact mass of each substance
mcqs.why: Qualitative analysis tells which substances are present in a sample. Quantity is the job of quantitative analysis, so options about amount, mass or volume describe quantitative work, not qualitative analysis.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of quantitative analysis?
mcqs.why: Titrimetric analysis is given in the notes as an example of quantitative analysis, along with gravimetric and combustion analysis. The flame test and chemical tests are examples of qualitative analysis because they only identify substances.

mcqs.q: Why must identification be done before quantification?
options: Because identification is cheaper than quantification
Because qualitative tests are always faster
Because if the compound is not identified, the method to measure its quantity cannot be chosen
Because quantity has no importance in analysis
mcqs.why: The notes explain that first it is necessary to know which compounds are in the sample, and only then can their quantity be determined. If the compound is not identified, the method to measure its quantity cannot be chosen, so identification always comes first.

mcqs.q: What does organic qualitative analysis deal with?
options: The identification of the presence of functional groups in compounds
The identification of ions and elements
mcqs.why: Organic qualitative analysis deals with the identification of the presence of functional groups in compounds. Identification of ions and elements belongs to inorganic qualitative analysis, while weighing and volume measurement are quantitative techniques.

mcqs.q: In inorganic qualitative analysis, what is identified?
mcqs.why: Inorganic qualitative analysis is the identification of ions and elements, such as in the flame test. Functional groups are identified in organic qualitative analysis, so that option belongs to the other type.

mcqs.q: In the flame test, a copper halide gives a bluish-green colour. What does this identify?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the flame test of copper halide with a bluish-green colour identifies the presence of halogen. The test is qualitative, so it identifies a substance rather than measuring any quantity.

mcqs.q: In what forms may a sample be during qualitative analysis?
options: Solid, liquid, gas or a mixture
mcqs.why: The notes say that in qualitative analysis the sample may be solid, liquid, gas or a mixture. It is therefore not restricted to any single physical state.

mcqs.q: Which pair correctly matches the type of analysis with what it tells?
options: Qualitative — quantity present; Quantitative — substances present
Qualitative — substances present; Quantitative — quantity present
mcqs.why: Qualitative analysis tells which substances are present in a sample, while quantitative analysis tells in what quantity those substances are present. The first option reverses the two, and the others wrongly make both types do the same job.

lessons.title: Important Parameters
lessons.notes_html:
Error

  • Systematic (determinate) error: an error that occurs in the same way every time and can be estimated and eliminated. Example: improper functioning of an instrument, and improper functioning in acid-base titration, such as a wrong burette reading or a wrong indicator — these produce an error in the same direction in every measurement.
  • Indeterminate error: an error that occurs randomly and is different every time.
  • Examples of errors in everyday life: a wrong weight on a weighing machine, a clock running fast or slow, measuring a wrong length with a measuring tape, reading a wrong temperature on a thermometer.

Accuracy and Precision

TermMeaning
AccuracyAgreement between a measured value and the accepted true value
PrecisionAgreement between replicate measurements of the same quantity, that is the repeatability of a result

A measurement can be precise but not accurate, accurate but not precise, both or neither.

Example: Volumes of a Gas (True Value 32 cm^3)

SetValuesResult
First32, 45, 17, 23Neither — the values are scattered
Second32, 33, 34, 35Accurate but not precise — close to the true value but not repeatable
Third32, 45, 45, 32Neither — the values are scattered
Fourth32, 32, 33, 32Accurate and precise both — repeatable and close to the true value

mcqs.q: What is a systematic (determinate) error?
options: An error that occurs in the same way every time and can be estimated and eliminated
An error that occurs randomly and is different every time
An error that can never be detected
An error caused only by carelessness
mcqs.why: A systematic or determinate error occurs in the same way every time and can be estimated and eliminated. An error that occurs randomly and differs each time is an indeterminate error, which is the opposite type.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of a systematic error?
options: A clock running at a varying speed each day
Reading a scale from a different angle each time
mcqs.why: Improper functioning of an instrument is given as an example of systematic error because it produces an error in the same direction in every measurement. Random, varying mistakes belong to indeterminate error instead.

mcqs.q: In acid-base titration, which faults produce systematic error?
options: A wrong burette reading or a wrong indicator
mcqs.why: The notes give improper functioning in acid-base titration, such as a wrong burette reading or a wrong indicator, as a source of systematic error. These faults push every measurement in the same direction, unlike the careful practices listed in the other options.

mcqs.q: What is an indeterminate error?
options: An error that occurs in the same way every time
An error that can always be eliminated
An error in the instrument's design
An error that occurs randomly and is different every time
mcqs.why: An indeterminate error occurs randomly and is different every time, so it cannot be predicted or removed in the way a systematic error can. Occurring the same way every time describes systematic error, not indeterminate error.

mcqs.q: Which of these is listed as an everyday example of error?
options: A wrong weight on a weighing machine
mcqs.why: The notes list a wrong weight on a weighing machine, a clock running fast or slow, a wrong length with a measuring tape and a wrong temperature on a thermometer as everyday examples of errors. The other options describe correct measurements, not errors.

mcqs.q: What does accuracy mean?
options: Agreement between a measured value and the accepted true value
Agreement between replicate measurements of the same quantity
mcqs.why: Accuracy is the agreement between a measured value and the accepted true value. Agreement between repeated measurements of the same quantity is precision, so that option defines the wrong term.

mcqs.q: What does precision mean?
options: Agreement between a measured value and the true value
How close a result is to the accepted value
Agreement between replicate measurements of the same quantity, i.e. repeatability
mcqs.why: Precision is the agreement between replicate measurements of the same quantity, that is, the repeatability of a result. Closeness to the accepted true value is accuracy, which is a different parameter.

mcqs.q: Which statement about accuracy and precision is correct?
options: A measurement must always be both accurate and precise
A measurement can be precise but not accurate, accurate but not precise, both or neither
Precision and accuracy are exactly the same thing
An accurate measurement is always repeatable
mcqs.why: The notes state that a measurement can be precise but not accurate, accurate but not precise, both accurate and precise, or neither. Accuracy and precision are therefore independent qualities, not the same thing.

mcqs.q: The true value of a gas volume is 32 cm^3. A set of readings is 32, 45, 17, 23. How is this set described?
options: Neither accurate nor precise — the values are scattered
mcqs.why: The readings 32, 45, 17 and 23 are widely scattered around the true value of 32 cm^3, so the set is neither accurate nor precise. The notes describe this first set exactly as 'Neither — the values are scattered'.

mcqs.q: The true value is 32 cm^3 and the readings are 32, 32, 33, 32. This set is:
options: Precise but far from the true value
mcqs.why: The readings 32, 32, 33 and 32 are repeatable and close to the true value of 32 cm^3, so the set is both accurate and precise. The notes describe this fourth set as 'Accurate and precise both'.

lessons.title: Classical Methods
lessons.notes_html:
What are Classical Methods?

Classical methods are traditional analytical methods based on chemical reactions and simple measurements. They are simple and cheap but slow and need a large amount of sample.

Titration

Titration is the technique in which the concentration of an unknown solution is determined by comparing the volume of a solution of known concentration with the volume of the solution of unknown concentration.

  • Burette: which contains the titrant (solution of known concentration).
  • Flask: which contains the analyte (substance being analysed).
  • Pipette: for taking a measured quantity.
  • Indicator: which changes its colour at the end point and tells that the titration is complete and the equivalence point has been reached.

Titrimetric and Gravimetric Analysis

TitrimetricGravimetric
Based on the measurement of volumeBased on the measurement of weight
The volume of a solution of known concentration is usedThe substance is converted into a product and then weighed

Steps of Gravimetric Analysis

  • Preparation of a solution with known weight of sample
  • Separation of the desired constituent
  • Weighing the separated constituent
  • Computation of the amount of the separated constituent in the sample

Comparison of Classical and Instrumental Methods

Techniques are compared on the basis of speed, accuracy, precision, amount of sample, cost and training. The classical method is simple and cheap but slow; the instrumental method is fast, sensitive and expensive and needs specialized training.

mcqs.q: What are classical methods of analysis?
options: Traditional analytical methods based on chemical reactions and simple measurements
Methods based on modern electronic instruments
Methods that need only a tiny amount of sample
mcqs.why: Classical methods are traditional analytical methods based on chemical reactions and simple measurements. They are simple and cheap, but slow, and they need a large amount of sample rather than a tiny one.

mcqs.q: Which statement about classical methods is correct?
options: They are simple and cheap but slow and need a large amount of sample
mcqs.why: The notes describe classical methods as simple and cheap but slow, needing a large amount of sample. Being fast, sensitive, expensive and needing specialized training are features of instrumental methods instead.

mcqs.q: What is titration?
options: Weighing a substance after converting it into a product
The technique in which the concentration of an unknown solution is determined by comparing the volumes of a known and an unknown solution
Heating a sample until it burns
mcqs.why: Titration is the technique in which the concentration of an unknown solution is determined by comparing the volume of a solution of known concentration with the volume of the solution of unknown concentration. Weighing a converted product describes gravimetric analysis instead.

mcqs.q: In a titration, what is the titrant and where is it placed?
options: The substance being analysed, placed in the flask
The indicator, placed in the pipette
The unknown solution, placed in the burette
The solution of known concentration, placed in the burette
mcqs.why: The burette contains the titrant, which is the solution of known concentration. The flask contains the analyte, the substance being analysed, so the first option swaps the two solutions and their vessels.

mcqs.q: What is the analyte in a titration?
options: The substance being analysed, kept in the flask
mcqs.why: The analyte is the substance being analysed, and it is kept in the flask during a titration. The solution of known concentration is the titrant, and the colour-changing substance is the indicator.

mcqs.q: What is the role of the indicator in a titration?
options: It changes its colour at the end point and tells that the titration is complete
It measures the volume of the solution
It takes a measured quantity of solution
mcqs.why: The indicator changes its colour at the end point and tells that the titration is complete and the equivalence point has been reached. Measuring volumes and holding solutions are jobs of the burette, pipette and flask.

mcqs.q: What is the pipette used for in titration?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the pipette is used for taking a measured quantity. The burette holds the titrant, and the indicator detects the end point, so those options assign the pipette the wrong job.

mcqs.q: How does titrimetric analysis differ from gravimetric analysis?
options: Titrimetric is based on weight; gravimetric is based on volume
Titrimetric is based on the measurement of volume; gravimetric is based on the measurement of weight
mcqs.why: Titrimetric analysis is based on the measurement of volume, using the volume of a solution of known concentration. Gravimetric analysis is based on the measurement of weight, where the substance is converted into a product and then weighed.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a step of gravimetric analysis?
options: Adding an indicator to the flask
Reading the burette at the end point
mcqs.why: The steps of gravimetric analysis are: preparation of a solution with a known weight of sample, separation of the desired constituent, weighing the separated constituent, and computation of its amount in the sample. Indicators and burette readings belong to titration.

mcqs.q: On what basis are classical and instrumental techniques compared?
options: Speed, accuracy, precision, amount of sample, cost and training
Only on the colour of results
Only on the size of the laboratory
mcqs.why: Techniques are compared on the basis of speed, accuracy, precision, amount of sample, cost and training. On these grounds the classical method is simple and cheap but slow, while the instrumental method is fast, sensitive and expensive and needs specialized training.

lessons.title: Modern Instrumental Methods
lessons.notes_html:
Instrumental Methods

Instrumental methods measure the physical properties of substances with modern instruments. They are more effective than classical methods because they are very fast, sensitive, work with a small amount of sample, and give both identification and quantity in less time. They can also analyse trace amounts and work automatically. In contrast, classical methods are slow and accuracy decreases with decreasing amount of sample.

Spectroscopy

  • Spectroscopy is the interaction of light with matter.
  • It is used to assess the concentration or amount of a given atomic, molecular or ionic chemical.
  • Physical methods deal with the physical properties of substances, such as atomic emission spectroscopy, Fourier transform spectroscopy and X-ray spectroscopy.
  • Ultraviolet and visible spectroscopy and infrared spectroscopy are its types.
  • Infrared spectroscopy tells the identification and quantity of samples in less time and at less cost, and no polluting chemical is required for it; it is used for the identification of functional groups in food products, polymers and industries and for quality control.

Chromatography

  • Chromatography is a method for the separation of compounds; types: high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and gas chromatography.
  • Gas chromatography is a method for the separation of gases and volatile compounds; the separation takes place by the exchange between a mobile gas phase and a liquid or solid stationary phase. Gas is the mobile phase in it.
  • Instruments: gas cylinder, sample injector, gas chromatograph column, detector and data collection device. The detector detects the elution of compounds and sends signals to the computer.
  • Uses: inorganic compounds, carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, pollutants like benzene, plastic materials and dairy products.

Electrochemical Methods

  • These methods measure the potential, charge and electrical quantity of a solution, and these measurements are carried out with an electrochemical cell.
  • The cell has two half cells with anode and cathode electrodes, connected by a salt bridge. At the anode electrons are liberated in oxidation and at the cathode electrons are consumed in reduction.
  • Potentiometry: the potential between two electrodes is measured by a voltmeter and there is no flow of current; it is used to find the concentration of a solute in solution, pollutants in water, pharmaceuticals and drugs, quality control in the food industry and clinical chemistry.
  • Applications of conductometry: the dissociation constant can be determined, the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt can be determined, the rate constant of a reaction can be studied, and the end point of titration can be determined.

mcqs.q: What do instrumental methods measure?
options: The physical properties of substances with modern instruments
mcqs.why: Instrumental methods measure the physical properties of substances with modern instruments. They are more effective than classical methods because they are very fast and sensitive, which weighing precipitates and other classical steps are not.

mcqs.q: Why are instrumental methods more effective than classical methods?
options: They are cheaper and need no training
They are very fast, sensitive, work with a small amount of sample and give identification and quantity in less time
mcqs.why: Instrumental methods are very fast, sensitive, work with a small amount of sample, and give both identification and quantity in less time; they can also analyse trace amounts and work automatically. Classical methods are the slow ones whose accuracy decreases with decreasing amount of sample.

mcqs.q: What is spectroscopy?
options: The separation of compounds by a column
The interaction of light with matter
The weighing of a separated constituent
mcqs.why: Spectroscopy is the interaction of light with matter, used to assess the concentration or amount of a given atomic, molecular or ionic chemical. Separation by a column is chromatography, and potential measurement is an electrochemical method.

mcqs.q: Which of these are types of spectroscopy mentioned in the notes?
options: Ultraviolet and visible spectroscopy and infrared spectroscopy
mcqs.why: Ultraviolet and visible spectroscopy and infrared spectroscopy are types of spectroscopy, and physical methods also include atomic emission, Fourier transform and X-ray spectroscopy. HPLC and gas chromatography are chromatography types, while potentiometry and conductometry are electrochemical methods.

mcqs.q: What is infrared spectroscopy used for?
options: The identification of functional groups in food products, polymers and industries, and for quality control
mcqs.why: Infrared spectroscopy is used for the identification of functional groups in food products, polymers and industries and for quality control. It identifies samples and their quantity in less time and at less cost, and no polluting chemical is required for it.

mcqs.q: What is chromatography used for?
options: The measurement of potential between electrodes
The interaction of light with matter
mcqs.why: Chromatography is a method for the separation of compounds, with types such as high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and gas chromatography. Interaction of light with matter is spectroscopy, not chromatography.

mcqs.q: In gas chromatography, what is the mobile phase?
mcqs.why: In gas chromatography the separation of gases and volatile compounds takes place by the exchange between a mobile gas phase and a liquid or solid stationary phase. Gas is the mobile phase, while the liquid or solid forms the stationary phase.

mcqs.q: What is the function of the detector in a gas chromatograph?
options: It supplies the gas to the column
It detects the elution of compounds and sends signals to the computer
mcqs.why: The detector detects the elution of compounds and sends signals to the computer. The gas cylinder supplies the gas and the sample injector introduces the sample, so those instruments have different functions.

mcqs.q: What do electrochemical methods measure?
options: Only the colour change of an indicator
The boiling point of a liquid
The potential, charge and electrical quantity of a solution
mcqs.why: Electrochemical methods measure the potential, charge and electrical quantity of a solution, and these measurements are carried out with an electrochemical cell. Colour changes, boiling points and precipitate masses belong to other techniques.

mcqs.q: In potentiometry, how is the potential measured?
options: By a voltmeter, with current flowing freely
By a voltmeter, with no flow of current
mcqs.why: In potentiometry the potential between two electrodes is measured by a voltmeter and there is no flow of current. It is used to find the concentration of a solute in solution, pollutants in water, pharmaceuticals and drugs, quality control in the food industry and clinical chemistry.

lessons.title: Preparation of Soap
lessons.notes_html:
What is Soap?

Soaps are salts of fatty acids. Soap molecules reduce the surface tension of water; such substances are called surfactants.

Two Ends of the Soap Molecule

EndProperty
Carboxylate endHydrophilic — is attracted to water
Hydrocarbon endHydrophobic — is attracted to oil and dirt

Saponification

Saponification is the chemical reaction in which fat or oil reacts with caustic soda NaOH or caustic potash KOH to form soap and glycerine.

  • NaOH gives hard soap.
  • KOH gives soft soap, because potassium soaps are more soluble in water.

Stages of Preparation (Flow Sheet)

  • 1. Oil or fat
  • 2. Bleaching, refining, deodorization
  • 3. Saponification — aqueous NaOH is added
  • 4. Separation — NaCl brine is added and glycerine is separated
  • 5. Purification — citric acid is added
  • 6. Finishing — fragrances, conservative agent and colouring are added
  • 7. Soap is prepared

mcqs.q: What are soaps chemically?
mcqs.why: Soaps are salts of fatty acids. They are formed when fat or oil reacts with an alkali such as caustic soda or caustic potash during saponification.

mcqs.q: Substances like soap that reduce the surface tension of water are called:
mcqs.why: Soap molecules reduce the surface tension of water, and such substances are called surfactants. This surface-tension-reducing property is what makes soap useful for cleaning.

mcqs.q: Which end of the soap molecule is hydrophilic?
mcqs.why: The carboxylate end of the soap molecule is hydrophilic, meaning it is attracted to water. The hydrocarbon end is the opposite: it is hydrophobic and is attracted to oil and dirt.

mcqs.q: The hydrocarbon end of a soap molecule is attracted to:
mcqs.why: The hydrocarbon end is hydrophobic and is attracted to oil and dirt, which is how soap lifts grease from surfaces. The carboxylate end is the one attracted to water, not the hydrocarbon end.

mcqs.q: What is saponification?
options: The reaction of fat or oil with water to form glycerine only
The chemical reaction in which fat or oil reacts with caustic soda NaOH or caustic potash KOH to form soap and glycerine
The separation of soap with brine
mcqs.why: Saponification is the chemical reaction in which fat or oil reacts with caustic soda NaOH or caustic potash KOH to form soap and glycerine. Bleaching and brine separation are other stages of soap preparation, not the saponification reaction itself.

mcqs.q: Which alkali gives hard soap?
mcqs.why: NaOH gives hard soap. KOH gives soft soap instead, because potassium soaps are more soluble in water than sodium soaps.

mcqs.q: Why does KOH give soft soap?
options: Because potassium soaps are less soluble in water
Because KOH is a weaker alkali
Because potassium soaps are more soluble in water
mcqs.why: KOH gives soft soap because potassium soaps are more soluble in water. Their greater solubility makes the resulting soap softer, unlike the hard soap obtained from NaOH.

mcqs.q: In the flow sheet of soap preparation, what is added at the separation stage?
mcqs.why: At the separation stage NaCl brine is added and glycerine is separated. Citric acid is added later at the purification stage, and fragrances are added at the finishing stage.

mcqs.q: What is added during the purification stage of soap making?
mcqs.why: Citric acid is added at the purification stage of soap preparation. Aqueous NaOH is added during saponification, brine during separation, and colouring at the finishing stage.

mcqs.q: What happens at the finishing stage of soap preparation?
options: Fragrances, conservative agent and colouring are added
mcqs.why: At the finishing stage, fragrances, conservative agent and colouring are added, after which the soap is prepared. Bleaching, refining and deodorization happen before saponification, and glycerine is separated earlier with brine.

lessons.title: Preparation of Sugar from Sugarcane
lessons.notes_html:
Raw Material

The raw material for the preparation of sugar is: sugarcane, lime and water. Harvesting of sugarcane is the most important step in the preparation of sugar.

Stages of Preparation

  • 1. Harvesting and delivery: Sugarcane is harvested in the cooler months and sent to the factory.
  • 2. Juice extraction: The cane is cut into chips and the juice is extracted in mills.
  • 3. Clarification: Heat, lime and flocculation aids are added to the juice; lime is a suspension of calcium hydroxide which kills enzymes and brings the pH from 5.0 to 6.5 to neutral; mud is separated. Bagasse is the fibre which does not dissolve in water.
  • 4. Concentration: The clarified juice is heated in evaporators and sucrose is increased from 10 to 15 percent to 55 to 59 percent.
  • 5. Crystallization: The syrup is further evaporated in vacuum pans, seed crystals are added, and sugar crystals form.
  • 6. Crystal separation and drying: The crystals are separated from molasses in a basket-type centrifuge machine and dried.

mcqs.q: What are the raw materials for the preparation of sugar?
mcqs.why: The raw material for the preparation of sugar is sugarcane, lime and water. Lime is used again during clarification, where it is added to the juice along with heat and flocculation aids.

mcqs.q: Which step is described as the most important step in the preparation of sugar?
mcqs.why: Harvesting of sugarcane is the most important step in the preparation of sugar. The cane is harvested in the cooler months and then sent to the factory for the later stages.

mcqs.q: When is sugarcane harvested and where is it sent?
options: In the hotter months, to storage
In the cooler months, to the factory
At any time, to the fields
In the rainy season, to the market
mcqs.why: Sugarcane is harvested in the cooler months and sent to the factory. There the cane is cut into chips and the juice is extracted in mills.

mcqs.q: How is juice extracted from sugarcane?
options: The cane is boiled in water
The cane is dried and ground
The juice is pressed out by hand
The cane is cut into chips and the juice is extracted in mills
mcqs.why: In the juice extraction stage the cane is cut into chips and the juice is extracted in mills. The extracted juice then goes to clarification, where heat, lime and flocculation aids are added.

mcqs.q: What is lime, as used in the clarification of cane juice?
mcqs.why: Lime is a suspension of calcium hydroxide. Added during clarification, it kills enzymes and brings the pH of the juice from 5.0 to 6.5 to neutral, after which the mud is separated.

mcqs.q: What does lime do to the pH of cane juice during clarification?
options: It brings the pH from 5.0 to 6.5 to neutral
It lowers the pH from 6.5 to 5.0
It makes the juice strongly alkaline
It does not affect the pH
mcqs.why: Lime kills enzymes and brings the pH from 5.0 to 6.5 to neutral during clarification. The juice starts acidic at 5.0, so lime raises it toward neutral rather than lowering it.

mcqs.q: What is bagasse?
options: The seed crystals used in pans
The fibre which does not dissolve in water
mcqs.why: Bagasse is the fibre which does not dissolve in water. It is the fibrous residue of the cane, distinct from the mud separated in clarification and from the syrup formed during concentration.

mcqs.q: During concentration, sucrose in the clarified juice is increased from 10–15 percent to:
mcqs.why: In the concentration stage the clarified juice is heated in evaporators and sucrose is increased from 10 to 15 percent to 55 to 59 percent. The concentrated syrup then goes to vacuum pans for crystallization.

mcqs.q: How are sugar crystals formed during crystallization?
options: The juice is filtered through cloth
The syrup is further evaporated in vacuum pans and seed crystals are added
The syrup is mixed with molasses
mcqs.why: During crystallization the syrup is further evaporated in vacuum pans, seed crystals are added, and sugar crystals form. The crystals are afterwards separated from molasses and dried.

mcqs.q: How are sugar crystals separated from molasses?
mcqs.why: The crystals are separated from molasses in a basket-type centrifuge machine and then dried. This is the final stage of sugar preparation given in the notes.

lessons.title: Preparation of Soft Drinks
lessons.notes_html:
Components of Soft Drinks

The basis of soft drinks is syrup, which is made up of water, sugar, acid, colouring and flavouring agents. The components are:

  • Water, calcium and other minerals
  • Colouring and flavouring agent
  • Sugar for microbial growth
  • Citric acid for sour taste

The syrup is prepared by dissolving the ingredients into water to 65 Brix.

Stages of Preparation

  • Stage 1 — Water cleaning: Raw water is passed through a filter, water softener, chemicals and pump.
  • Stage 2 — Heating, evaporation and carbonation: The water is heated with electric heaters, passed through a cooling pipe, and carbon dioxide is added to make carbonated water.
  • Stage 3 — Mixing: Colouring, syrup and flavour are added in the mixing tank.
  • Stage 4 — Filtering and filling: The drink is filtered and filled into bottles and cans.
  • Stage 5 — Packaging: Packed in cartons and sent to the supermarket.

mcqs.q: What is the basis of soft drinks?
options: Syrup, made up of water, sugar, acid, colouring and flavouring agents
mcqs.why: The basis of soft drinks is syrup, which is made up of water, sugar, acid, colouring and flavouring agents. Carbonated water is prepared in a later stage and mixed with this syrup.

mcqs.q: Which component of a soft drink gives the sour taste?
mcqs.why: Citric acid is the component added for the sour taste in soft drinks. Sugar is listed for microbial growth, while colouring and flavouring agents serve other purposes.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, what role is sugar listed with in soft drink components?
mcqs.why: The components list gives sugar for microbial growth, while citric acid provides the sour taste. Colour comes from colouring agents and carbonation from carbon dioxide added in stage 2, so those options name other components' roles.

mcqs.q: To how many Brix is the syrup prepared by dissolving the ingredients into water?
mcqs.why: The syrup is prepared by dissolving the ingredients into water to 65 Brix. This concentrated syrup is then used in the mixing stage of soft drink preparation.

mcqs.q: What happens in Stage 1 of soft drink preparation?
options: Carbon dioxide is added to the water
The drink is filled into bottles
Raw water is passed through a filter, water softener, chemicals and pump
mcqs.why: Stage 1 is water cleaning: raw water is passed through a filter, water softener, chemicals and pump. Adding carbon dioxide belongs to stage 2, mixing to stage 3, and filling to stage 4.

mcqs.q: In Stage 2, what is added to the water to make carbonated water?
mcqs.why: In stage 2 the water is heated with electric heaters, passed through a cooling pipe, and carbon dioxide is added to make carbonated water. Citric acid is part of the syrup, not the gas used for carbonation.

mcqs.q: How is the water heated in Stage 2 of soft drink preparation?
mcqs.why: The notes state that in stage 2 the water is heated with electric heaters and then passed through a cooling pipe before carbon dioxide is added. No other heating method is mentioned for this stage.

mcqs.q: What happens in Stage 3 (mixing) of soft drink preparation?
options: Colouring, syrup and flavour are added in the mixing tank
The drink is packed in cartons
mcqs.why: In stage 3, colouring, syrup and flavour are added in the mixing tank. Carbonation happens in stage 2, and packing in cartons is the final stage 5.

mcqs.q: What happens in Stage 4 of soft drink preparation?
options: The syrup is prepared to 65 Brix
The drink is filtered and filled into bottles and cans
The cartons are sent to the supermarket
mcqs.why: Stage 4 is filtering and filling: the drink is filtered and filled into bottles and cans. Sending packed cartons to the supermarket is stage 5, the packaging stage.

mcqs.q: What is done in the final stage (Stage 5) of soft drink preparation?
options: The product is packed in cartons and sent to the supermarket
mcqs.why: Stage 5 is packaging: the product is packed in cartons and sent to the supermarket. All the earlier steps — cleaning, carbonation, mixing, filtering and filling — are completed before this final stage.

lessons.title: Petroleum Industry
lessons.notes_html:
What is Petroleum?

Petroleum is a natural substance trapped in rocks beneath the earth's crust. Petroleum means rock oil. It is a complex combination of gaseous, liquid and solid hydrocarbons, in which water, salts and earth particles are also present. It is a liquid lighter than water and does not dissolve in it.

Black Gold

Petroleum is called Black Gold because it is black and as valuable as gold. From it petrol, diesel, kerosene, gas, plastics and many other things are obtained. It is the main source of the economy and energy of countries.

Fractional Distillation and Fractions

Petroleum is separated into fractions by fractional distillation, which is done in refineries in fractionating columns — the column is cold at the top and hot at the bottom.

FractionBoiling range (C)CarbonsUse
Refinery gas-160 to -51 to 4Home heating and cooking
Petrol40 to 1105 to 8Car fuel
